    available_excerpt: "# Harbor 2 matter dossier\n\n## Current position\n\nThe Harbor
      Pay migration needs legal and compliance review before the planned Nov 15 close.
      This is the accepted working view. It is not a recorded decision.\n\nThis draft
      recommends separating the acquisition closing from the launch of regulated services.
      The asset purchase can proceed while Mosaic prepares for migration. However,
      Mosaic should not give all Harbor users full access on day one unless these
      conditions are met:\n\n1. Mosaic has documented authority for each post-close
      service in each affected state.\n2. Compliance confirms how Mosaic can use Harbor’s
      prior know-your-customer (KYC) results and remedy missing records.\n3. Authorized
      reviewers assess Harbor’s open alerts and suspicious activity report (SAR) history.\n4.
      Mosaic validates the replacement transaction-monitoring feed without a coverage
      gap.\n\nIf a condition is not met, Mosaic should hold the affected state launch,
      restrict affected accounts, or delay full product access. The planned $50 welcome
      bonus should wait until its structure, terms, and disclosures are reviewed.\n\nNo
      decision has been recorded.\n\n### Assumptions used\n\n- Harbor is a licensed
      money transmitter subject to applicable state and federal anti-money-laundering
      requirements. The licensing, KYC, alert, and monitoring answers depend on this
      unverified premise.\n- Mosaic will become the operating provider after close.
      This affects whether Harbor could remain the licensed provider during a transition.\n-
      This analysis does not assume that Harbor’s licenses transfer, that its KYC
      results satisfy Mosaic’s program, or that monitoring can continue without a
      gap.\n- Mosaic’s 41-state license footprint is a reported fact. It is not treated
      as an assumption.\n- The acquisition is a reported asset purchase. The older
      assumption that its structure was unknown is superseded by that reported answer.\n\n###
      Record conflicts\n\n- Harbor reportedly has licenses in 38 states, Mosaic has
      licenses in 41 states, and the combined footprint is 44 states. A 44-state footprint
      is three states larger than Mosaic’s 41-state footprint, but the record says
      the acquisition opens four new markets. This affects which states need separate
      authority or launch restrictions. The two license lists and the intended meaning
      of “market” are needed.\n- Matter metadata gives a target date of `2026-09-11`.
      The reported close is “Nov 15,” approximately ten weeks after the Sept. 9 intake.
      A saved hypothetical uses November 15, 2026, but that does not establish the
      actual closing year. The operative close date and year remain unresolved.\n\n##
      Decision question\n\nDoes any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need
      legal review before the Nov 15 close?\n\n## Issues\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045
      -->\n### Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under
      the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor's MTLs transfer/survive the
      acquisition\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic should not treat Harbor’s money
      transmitter licenses as assets that automatically transfer in the asset purchase.
      Mosaic should not launch regulated services in a state without documented authority
      for its complete post-close activity.\n\nThe acquisition may close separately
      from the service launch. A state launch hold is the current fallback where authority
      is not established.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThe saved research concludes
      that the answer must be determined state by state. The review must cover Mosaic’s
      authority, transaction notices or approvals, interim operation, outstanding
      obligations, and Harbor’s license surrender.\n\nFour sources were retrieved,
      but no operative passage was read or verified. They do not establish the governing
      rule in any affected state:\n\n- [Money transmission research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
      [CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538-157583424427.md)\n-
      [New York Department of Financial Services licensing page — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4-fa80c95c5393.md)\n-
      [OCC commentary — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413-e75b998a6dec.md)\n-
      [Fenergo licensing overview — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200-fcb5e16956fb.md)\n\nThe
      model act is not proof of any specific state’s law. The premise that an asset
      purchase does not automatically give Mosaic Harbor’s operating authority remains
      an unverified state-law conclusion.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor reportedly
      has licenses in 38 states. Mosaic reportedly has licenses in 41 states. Their
      combined footprint is reported as 44 states. Mosaic plans to use or assume Harbor’s
      licenses in the new markets.\n\nThe unified Mosaic account, combined balance,
      and access to Mosaic products suggest that Mosaic may become the actual service
      provider. If so, keeping Harbor’s entity or licenses active might not authorize
      Mosaic’s conduct.\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider during a transition
      only if the customer contracts, funds flow, operating control, licenses, bonds,
      records, and applicable state rules support that result. The structure must
      match actual operations.\n\nA partner bank holding funds would not by itself
      resolve the issue. The result still depends on who contracts with users, controls
      transfers, owes repayment, records balances, resolves errors, and performs the
      regulated duties.\n\n**Next step**\n\nIdentify the Harbor-only jurisdictions
      and complete one state matrix. It should address Mosaic’s authority, required
      filings and approvals, operation while an application is pending, transfer of
      customer obligations, bank custody and control, Harbor’s run-off duties, and
      the required launch restriction if authority is not established.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:start
      -->\n<details>\n<summary>Saved research and prior analysis</summary>\n\nPreserved
      research snapshot. Its facts and assumptions may predate later records. Use
      the current answer above for application to the current matter.\n\nDo not rely
      on transferability without an applicable state rule, approval, or written regulator
      position.\n\nThe answer must be determined state by state and must cover more
      than technical change-of-control rules.\n\nThis path is possible only if Harbor
      remains the real provider and the relevant states permit the arrangement. The
      unified Mosaic account design may conflict with that position.\n\nThe result
      depends on the contracts and actual funds flow. Custody alone should not be
      treated as a licensing exemption or transfer mechanism.\n\nResearch saved. 4
      sources retrieved; 0 with passages read.\n\nNext step: Identify the four Harbor-only
      states and complete one matrix covering license authority, transaction filings,
      interim operation, bank custody, outstanding obligations, and license surrender.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Detailed
      analysis</summary>\n\n**Practical answer**\n\n**Do not treat Harbor’s money
      transmitter licenses as assets that move to Mosaic in the asset purchase.**
      Use this closing rule:\n\n> **No confirmed authority means no regulated launch
      by Mosaic in that state.**\n\nThe asset purchase can still close. However, Mosaic
      should not activate regulated services in the four Harbor-only states unless
      one of these conditions is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its own license.\n2. The
      state approves a transfer or other license change.\n3. The regulator confirms
      a lawful interim structure.\n4. Harbor remains the real licensed provider under
      a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic blocks regulated functions in that state.\n\nThe
      planned unified Mosaic account is important. It suggests that Mosaic, not Harbor,
      will become the service provider. If that is correct, keeping Harbor’s legal
      entity and licenses alive might not give Mosaic authority to operate.\n\n**No
      verified operative authority retrieved.** The collection found the CSBS Model
      Money Transmission Modernization Act and a New York regulator licensing page.
      However, no exact provision about an asset sale, license transfer, interim operation,
      or custody was available for review. Also, a model act is not proof of the law
      adopted in a specific state. The state-specific conclusions below remain conditional.\n\n**Work
      needed before launch**\n\n| Work | Why | Proposed owner | Needed by | Evidence
      to proceed | Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Identify the four Harbor-only
      states | These states have the clearest authority gap | Licensing team | Now
      | Confirmed license list and covered activities | Block regulated functions
      in those states |\n| Build a matrix for every affected state | Transfer, notice,
      approval, and surrender rules can differ | State regulatory counsel | Before
      the closing conditions are final | Applicable rule, filing deadline, regulator
      response, and license status | Delay migration in the affected state |\n| Confirm
      the post-close service provider | The licensed entity must match the actual
      operating model | Product and deal counsel | Before customer notices and account
      design are final | Contracts, user interface, funds-flow diagram, and operating
      roles | Keep Harbor as the actual provider where permitted |\n| Review notices
      and approvals | An asset sale can create separate seller and buyer requirements
      | Licensing team | Before each state deadline | Filing receipts and required
      approvals or non-objections | Make approval a state launch condition |\n| Confirm
      interim operating authority | A pending application should not be assumed to
      permit operation | State regulatory counsel | Before close | Applicable rule
      or written regulator confirmation | Keep Harbor customers segregated or restrict
      transactions |\n| Review partner-bank arrangements | Bank custody does not,
      by itself, establish Mosaic’s licensing position | Payments counsel and bank
      relationship owner | Before balances move | Bank agreements, account titles,
      control rights, reconciliation design, and bank consent | Keep funds and obligations
      in the existing structure |\n| Prepare license run-off and surrender plans |
      Harbor may retain duties for balances, claims, records, and reports | Harbor
      compliance and deal counsel | Before surrender or operational shutdown | Regulator-approved
      plan and continued bonds and financial coverage | Keep Harbor licensed and operational
      longer |\n\n**State notice and approval**\n\nDo not search only for a rule called
      “license transfer.” Review each state for:\n\n- sale of substantially all assets;\n-
      change of control;\n- change in business plan;\n- change in licensed activities;\n-
      assignment of outstanding payment obligations;\n- change in responsible persons,
      locations, or agents;\n- license surrender or termination;\n- customer agreement
      assignment; and\n- movement of stored balances or customer funds.\n\nAn asset
      purchase might fall outside a technical “change of control” rule because Harbor’s
      ownership does not change. That does not resolve the issue. Harbor might still
      need a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic might separately need authority
      before it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe state matrix should distinguish:\n\n-
      notice only;\n- approval before closing;\n- approval before customer migration;\n-
      new license required;\n- operation permitted while an application is pending;\n-
      regulator-approved transition available; and\n- no supported interim path.\n\n**Interim
      operation**\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider for a transition period.
      However, the structure must be real, not only contractual language.\n\nA supportable
      structure would normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor remains responsible
      to customers.\n- Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n- Harbor controls
      the regulated activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses, bonds, and financial
      coverage remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding obligations remain
      covered.\n- Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints, and examinations.\n-
      Required records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational role is permitted.\n-
      The partner bank accepts the structure.\n- Each relevant regulator permits or
      accepts the structure.\n\nThe present plan creates tension with this approach.
      A single Mosaic account, one combined balance, and full access to Mosaic products
      make it harder to show that Harbor remains the true provider.\n\n**Partner-bank
      custody**\n\nA partner bank account is not automatically a substitute for a
      money transmitter license. The key questions concern the complete activity and
      obligation flow.\n\nFor each customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1.
      Who receives the customer’s instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to transmit
      or return the funds?\n3. In whose name is the bank account held?\n4. Is it a
      custodial or “for benefit of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6. Who
      owns the ledger and resolves errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer fails?\n8.
      Which entity owes the customer a refund?\n9. Which entity’s license, bond, and
      permissible investments cover the obligation?\n10. Does the bank agreement permit
      assignment, migration, or a change in the program manager?\n11. Is bank consent
      required before closing or migration?\n12. What happens to funds if Harbor,
      Mosaic, or the bank relationship ends?\n\nA bank-led model might provide a different
      licensing analysis if the bank is the actual provider and Mosaic performs only
      permitted services. A bank account that merely holds funds for Mosaic or Harbor
      is different. The legal documents, customer terms, control rights, and actual
      operations must all support the claimed model.\n\nAlso review:\n\n- account
      segregation;\n- daily reconciliation;\n- shortfalls and reserve funding;\n-
      bank setoff rights;\n- liens and security interests;\n- continuity if the account
      is frozen;\n- treatment of pending transfers;\n- return and chargeback duties;\n-
      insolvency treatment;\n- customer disclosures; and\n- whether any deposit-insurance
      statement is accurate for the actual account structure.\n\n**Recommended closing
      position**\n\nKeep the acquisition closing separate from the regulated-service
      launch.\n\nFor the four Harbor-only states, use a state launch hold unless Mosaic
      has documented authority. For overlapping states, confirm that Mosaic’s existing
      licenses cover the complete post-close product set and funds flow.\n\nDo not
      surrender Harbor’s licenses or release its bonds until the applicable regulators
      permit it and all outstanding obligations have been assigned, completed, or
      placed into an approved run-off structure.\n\nThis investigation does not change
      the current recommendation. It adds one material point: **partner-bank custody
      is part of the licensing analysis, but custody alone does not cure an authority
      gap.**\n\n</details>\n\nResearch history: [Saved research 1](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n\n</details>\n<!--
      retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045
      -->\n### BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor's prior KYC (with missing
      underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay's independent
      CIP/AML obligations\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe current no-reverification plan
      is not ready for approval. Mosaic has not confirmed that its anti-money-laundering
      and customer identification program permits reliance on Harbor’s prior KYC.
      Pass/fail results alone may not provide the records or risk information that
      Mosaic needs.\n\nMosaic should not give an affected user unrestricted access
      unless compliance confirms that reliance is permitted and that the available
      records are sufficient, or a defined remediation process is complete.\n\n**Rule
      and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched. No saved authority establishes
      Mosaic’s precise federal duties or whether Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s checks
      after this asset purchase.\n\nThe unverified legal premise is that the entity
      providing the post-close financial service must follow its applicable customer
      identification, recordkeeping, risk-rating, and ongoing anti-money-laundering
      duties. The precise research question is whether Mosaic may adopt or rely on
      Harbor’s prior verification, and what records or remediation Mosaic must retain
      when the underlying identity documents are unavailable.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor
      verified the users through a vendor that closed in 2024. Mosaic has pass/fail
      results for all users but lacks the underlying documents for users onboarded
      before 2023. Mosaic’s compliance team has not confirmed whether its own program
      permits reliance.\n\nIf Mosaic’s program and applicable law permit reliance
      on Harbor’s process and retained results, Mosaic may be able to migrate some
      users without full reverification. Mosaic would still need evidence that the
      prior process, data, sanctions screening, risk rating, and records meet the
      applicable requirements.\n\nIf reliance is not permitted, or if the evidence
      is inadequate, Mosaic will need reverification or another approved remediation.
      Until then, it should restrict the affected accounts or delay their migration.
      This control does not resolve licensing, alert, or monitoring issues.\n\n**Next
      step**\n\nCompliance should document the applicable program rule, divide users
      into supported and unsupported groups, and define the evidence or reverification
      needed for each group. The result must support a clear migration rule for pre-2023
      users.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:start -->\nInitial
      analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:end
      -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38 -->\n### SAR and alert handling:
      obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor's ~40 open alerts and SARs, and
      successor liability\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe approximately 40 open alerts
      and recent SAR history require authorized review before Mosaic accepts the related
      users and activity without restrictions. The current record does not show whether
      the alerts are routine, overdue, linked to material misconduct, or relevant
      to the acquisition terms.\n\nA record gap does not prove a violation. However,
      unread alerts prevent Mosaic from assessing the risk it would take into its
      platform.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched. No
      saved authority establishes who must resolve Harbor’s existing alerts, make
      any required filing, retain related records, or perform continuing review after
      an asset purchase.\n\nThe unverified legal premise is that the responsible regulated
      entity must assess potentially suspicious activity and meet applicable reporting
      and recordkeeping duties. The precise research question is how those duties
      are divided between Harbor and Mosaic for pre-close conduct, transferred accounts,
      and post-close continuing activity.\n\nAccess to SAR material can be legally
      restricted. Diligence must use authorized reviewers and approved access controls.
      This analysis does not direct Harbor to disclose or transfer restricted material
      to an unauthorized person.\n\n**Application**\n\nDiligence identified about
      40 open alerts and “a handful” of SARs from the last year. None have been reviewed
      for this matter.\n\nOlder conduct may remain Harbor’s responsibility, while
      Mosaic may have duties for activity that continues after migration. The asset
      purchase documents can allocate work and cost between the parties, but contractual
      allocation may not change a regulator’s view of the responsible entity.\n\nIf
      the review finds overdue cases, connected accounts, control failures, or material
      undisclosed conduct, Mosaic may need account restrictions, remediation, revised
      closing protection, or a change to migration scope. If authorized review clears
      the cases and confirms proper handling, this obstacle becomes smaller but does
      not resolve KYC or monitoring continuity.\n\n**Next step**\n\nUse an authorized
      diligence team to triage the alerts and review permitted SAR-related information.
      Produce an aging and risk summary, assign each unresolved case to Harbor or
      Mosaic, and identify any effect on account migration or deal protection.\n\n<!--
      retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:start -->\nInitial analysis —
      no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:end
      -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542 -->\n### Monitoring vendor
      transition: continuity of transaction monitoring when the SaaS contract terminates
      at close\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic should validate the replacement transaction-monitoring
      feed before migrated users receive full access. Repointing the feed on day one
      without tested coverage creates a risk that transactions will not be captured,
      scored, or investigated correctly.\n\nIf validation is incomplete, the fallback
      should be continued Harbor coverage, a delayed migration, or transaction restrictions.
      The current record does not show that any fallback is available.\n\n**Rule and
      support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched. No saved authority states the
      precise monitoring duty that applies to Harbor or Mosaic.\n\nThe unverified
      legal premise is that the responsible regulated provider must operate monitoring
      that is suitable for its risks and can support alert review and required reporting.
      The precise research question is which monitoring and continuity duties apply
      to each entity at close and during migration.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s
      third-party monitoring contract ends at close. The plan is to repoint Harbor’s
      transaction feed to Mosaic’s engine on day one.\n\nTechnical connectivity alone
      is not sufficient. Validation should establish complete data capture, correct
      field mapping, suitable scenarios and thresholds, timely alert creation, case
      ownership, historical-data availability, reconciliation, and recovery from failed
      feeds.\n\nThis work depends on the operating-provider and KYC decisions. Mosaic’s
      engine must monitor the actual products, customer risks, and funds flow that
      will exist after close. It must also support any continuing review of Harbor’s
      open cases.\n\n**Next step**\n\nComplete an end-to-end test using representative
      Harbor activity. The result needed to proceed is documented data completeness,
      alert generation, case routing, reconciliation, and a tested failure procedure.\n\n<!--
      retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:start -->\nInitial analysis —
      no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:end
      -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66 -->\n### Marketing compliance:
      the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money transmission or consumer protection
      implications\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe bonus should not launch at close+1
      until its operating terms and disclosures are reviewed. The offer is lower priority
      than licensing, KYC, alerts, and monitoring, but its planned timing leaves little
      room to correct unclear or misleading terms.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis
      issue has not been researched. No saved authority establishes the rules that
      apply to the proposed promotion.\n\nThe unverified legal premise is that the
      offer must accurately state its eligibility, required transfer, payment timing,
      limits, exclusions, expiration, and any right to reverse the bonus. Its funds
      flow must also fit the approved account and licensing structure. The precise
      research question is which state promotion, consumer-protection, money-transmission,
      unclaimed-property, tax, and disclosure rules apply to the final design.\n\n**Application**\n\nThe
      only reported terms are a $50 bonus on the first transfer and a planned close+1
      launch. The record does not state:\n\n- who qualifies;\n- the minimum or type
      of transfer;\n- who funds the bonus;\n- when it becomes available;\n- whether
      withdrawal or account-duration limits apply;\n- whether the offer is limited
      by state;\n- how disputes, reversals, fraud, and tax reporting are handled;
      or\n- what the customer-facing disclosures will say.\n\nThese terms determine
      whether the campaign is accurate and operationally supportable. The campaign
      must also exclude any state or user group whose migration or service access
      is held.\n\n**Next step**\n\nMarketing should provide the final offer mechanics,
      customer terms, creative material, state scope, and funds flow. Legal and compliance
      should approve that package before launch. If approval is not complete, delay
      the campaign without delaying otherwise lawful migration work.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:start
      -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
      retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:end -->\n\n## Alternatives considered\n\n<!--
      alternative:SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4 -->\n### Bank-held funds timing test
      — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
      this test only, a bank would hold the relevant funds while Mosaic controlled
      transfer instructions. The arrangement would depend on contract completion and
      bank operating setup. The test uses a November 15, 2026 migration and December
      3, 2026 bank readiness date. It also assumes missing pre-2023 identity documents,
      40 pending alert cases, and monitoring that ends at close.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nBank
      custody could change part of the licensing and safeguarding analysis if the
      contracts, customer terms, control rights, and actual operations support a bank-led
      model.\n\n**Trade-offs and added risks**\n\nOn the test dates, bank integration
      would be ready 18 days after the assumed migration date. The option therefore
      makes the tested November 15 launch harder unless readiness moves earlier or
      migration moves later.\n\nMosaic would still control transfer instructions.
      Bank custody alone does not establish that the bank is the regulated service
      provider or that Mosaic may operate without its own authority.\n\n**Issues that
      remain**\n\nThe option does not resolve missing KYC documents, pending alerts,
      SAR handling, or replacement monitoring. It also depends on completed bank contracts
      and operating setup.\n\n**Next action**\n\nThe saved working note names Mara
      Chen to obtain a dated bank-readiness plan and confirm whether the bank can
      support November 15. This is saved scenario guidance, not an assignment or commitment.
      The note also calls for assigned plans covering identity records, alerts, and
      monitoring.\n\nUse this option only if the bank model is legally supportable
      and can be operational before the chosen migration date. Otherwise, use it as
      a later transition structure rather than a basis for the initial launch.\n\n<!--
      alternative:SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6 -->\n### Bank-held funds structure
      — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
      this hypothetical only, a partner bank holds customer funds.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nThe
      model could reduce part of Mosaic’s direct funds-custody role. It could support
      a different licensing analysis if the bank is the actual provider and Mosaic
      performs only permitted services.\n\n**Trade-offs and added risks**\n\nCustody
      alone does not resolve who conducts the regulated activity. The option adds
      dependency on bank agreements, consent, account setup, control rights, reconciliation,
      and operating readiness.\n\n**Issues that remain**\n\nThe following points remain
      open:\n\n- who contracts with users;\n- who controls transfer instructions and
      settlement;\n- who records balances and owes repayment;\n- how KYC, monitoring,
      alerts, SARs, privacy, and marketing duties are allocated; and\n- whether each
      affected state accepts the structure.\n\nThe option does not by itself resolve
      any KYC, alert, monitoring, or marketing issue.\n\n**Next action**\n\nPrepare
      the proposed customer, funds, instruction, settlement, ledger, loss, refund,
      and compliance flows. Compare them with the existing full day-one Mosaic model.
      Use the bank option only if those documents and actual operations establish
      a lawful bank-led structure and the bank can be ready on time.\n\n## Next actions\n\n1.
      **Resolve the state launch boundary.**  \n   **Deliverable:** A reconciled license
      list and state-by-state authority matrix.  \n   **Result needed:** Documented
      authority or an approved transition path for every planned post-close activity.
      \ \n   **Dependent activity:** Day-one service activation and customer notices.
      \ \n   **Fallback:** Hold regulated functions in any state without confirmed
      authority.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Licensing team with state regulatory
      counsel; start now and finish before closing conditions and launch scope are
      final.\n\n2. **Review the alerts and SAR history through authorized channels.**
      \ \n   **Deliverable:** An aging, risk, ownership, and remediation summary.
      \ \n   **Result needed:** Each open case has an authorized owner, required action,
      and migration treatment.  \n   **Dependent decision:** Which users can migrate
      without restrictions and whether deal protection must change.  \n   **Fallback:**
      Restrict affected accounts and preserve Harbor’s handling responsibilities where
      lawful.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Harbor and Mosaic anti-money-laundering
      leads with deal counsel; complete before migration approval.\n\n3. **Set the
      KYC migration rule.**  \n   **Deliverable:** A documented compliance position
      and user segmentation plan.  \n   **Result needed:** Evidence that reliance
      is permitted and records are sufficient, or a defined reverification process.
      \ \n   **Dependent activity:** Migration of pre-2023 users without restrictions.
      \ \n   **Fallback:** Reverify, restrict, or delay the affected accounts.  \n
      \  **Proposed owner and timing:** Mosaic compliance; complete before user migration
      rules and notices are final.\n\n4. **Validate transaction monitoring.**  \n
      \  **Deliverable:** End-to-end test results and a continuity procedure.  \n
      \  **Result needed:** Complete data capture, correct alert generation and routing,
      reconciliation, and tested recovery.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Full post-close
      transaction access.  \n   **Fallback:** Extend Harbor coverage if available,
      delay migration, or impose transaction limits.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:**
      Mosaic anti-money-laundering operations and engineering; finish before Harbor’s
      monitoring contract ends at close.\n\n5. **Review the welcome bonus.**  \n   **Deliverable:**
      Approved mechanics, terms, disclosures, state scope, and funds flow.  \n   **Result
      needed:** An accurate and operationally supportable offer that matches launch
      restrictions.  \n   **Dependent activity:** The planned close+1 campaign.  \n
      \  **Fallback:** Delay or narrow the campaign.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:**
      Marketing with consumer and payments counsel; complete after the permitted launch
      scope is known and before campaign release.\n\n## Current work product and supporting
      records\n\n- [Original request](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md)\n- [Reported
      facts](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md)\n- [Money transmission research
      packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n- [Prior
      dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-dc2adc8aaff5906e6734.md)\n\n[Open
      saved dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-3dc22f6f653187367a96.md)\n\nDossier
      generated and saved."

      role: assistant
      content: "# Harbor 2 matter dossier\n\n## Current position\n\nThe Harbor Pay
        migration needs legal and compliance review before the planned Nov 15 close.
        This is the accepted working view. It is not a recorded decision.\n\nThis
        draft recommends separating the acquisition closing from the launch of regulated
        services. The asset purchase can proceed while Mosaic prepares for migration.
        However, Mosaic should not give all Harbor users full access on day one unless
        these conditions are met:\n\n1. Mosaic has documented authority for each post-close
        service in each affected state.\n2. Compliance confirms how Mosaic can use
        Harbor’s prior know-your-customer (KYC) results and remedy missing records.\n3.
        Authorized reviewers assess Harbor’s open alerts and suspicious activity report
        (SAR) history.\n4. Mosaic validates the replacement transaction-monitoring
        feed without a coverage gap.\n\nIf a condition is not met, Mosaic should hold
        the affected state launch, restrict affected accounts, or delay full product
        access. The planned $50 welcome bonus should wait until its structure, terms,
        and disclosures are reviewed.\n\nNo decision has been recorded.\n\n### Assumptions
        used\n\n- Harbor is a licensed money transmitter subject to applicable state
        and federal anti-money-laundering requirements. The licensing, KYC, alert,
        and monitoring answers depend on this unverified premise.\n- Mosaic will become
        the operating provider after close. This affects whether Harbor could remain
        the licensed provider during a transition.\n- This analysis does not assume
        that Harbor’s licenses transfer, that its KYC results satisfy Mosaic’s program,
        or that monitoring can continue without a gap.\n- Mosaic’s 41-state license
        footprint is a reported fact. It is not treated as an assumption.\n- The acquisition
        is a reported asset purchase. The older assumption that its structure was
        unknown is superseded by that reported answer.\n\n### Record conflicts\n\n-
        Harbor reportedly has licenses in 38 states, Mosaic has licenses in 41 states,
        and the combined footprint is 44 states. A 44-state footprint is three states
        larger than Mosaic’s 41-state footprint, but the record says the acquisition
        opens four new markets. This affects which states need separate authority
        or launch restrictions. The two license lists and the intended meaning of
        “market” are needed.\n- Matter metadata gives a target date of `2026-09-11`.
        The reported close is “Nov 15,” approximately ten weeks after the Sept. 9
        intake. A saved hypothetical uses November 15, 2026, but that does not establish
        the actual closing year. The operative close date and year remain unresolved.\n\n##
        Decision question\n\nDoes any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration
        need legal review before the Nov 15 close?\n\n## Issues\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045
        -->\n### Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under
        the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor's MTLs transfer/survive
        the acquisition\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic should not treat Harbor’s
        money transmitter licenses as assets that automatically transfer in the asset
        purchase. Mosaic should not launch regulated services in a state without documented
        authority for its complete post-close activity.\n\nThe acquisition may close
        separately from the service launch. A state launch hold is the current fallback
        where authority is not established.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThe saved research
        concludes that the answer must be determined state by state. The review must
        cover Mosaic’s authority, transaction notices or approvals, interim operation,
        outstanding obligations, and Harbor’s license surrender.\n\nFour sources were
        retrieved, but no operative passage was read or verified. They do not establish
        the governing rule in any affected state:\n\n- [Money transmission research
        packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n- [CSBS
        Model Money Transmission Modernization Act — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538-157583424427.md)\n-
        [New York Department of Financial Services licensing page — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4-fa80c95c5393.md)\n-
        [OCC commentary — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413-e75b998a6dec.md)\n-
        [Fenergo licensing overview — retrieved only](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200-fcb5e16956fb.md)\n\nThe
        model act is not proof of any specific state’s law. The premise that an asset
        purchase does not automatically give Mosaic Harbor’s operating authority remains
        an unverified state-law conclusion.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor reportedly
        has licenses in 38 states. Mosaic reportedly has licenses in 41 states. Their
        combined footprint is reported as 44 states. Mosaic plans to use or assume
        Harbor’s licenses in the new markets.\n\nThe unified Mosaic account, combined
        balance, and access to Mosaic products suggest that Mosaic may become the
        actual service provider. If so, keeping Harbor’s entity or licenses active
        might not authorize Mosaic’s conduct.\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed
        provider during a transition only if the customer contracts, funds flow, operating
        control, licenses, bonds, records, and applicable state rules support that
        result. The structure must match actual operations.\n\nA partner bank holding
        funds would not by itself resolve the issue. The result still depends on who
        contracts with users, controls transfers, owes repayment, records balances,
        resolves errors, and performs the regulated duties.\n\n**Next step**\n\nIdentify
        the Harbor-only jurisdictions and complete one state matrix. It should address
        Mosaic’s authority, required filings and approvals, operation while an application
        is pending, transfer of customer obligations, bank custody and control, Harbor’s
        run-off duties, and the required launch restriction if authority is not established.\n\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:start -->\n<details>\n<summary>Saved
        research and prior analysis</summary>\n\nPreserved research snapshot. Its
        facts and assumptions may predate later records. Use the current answer above
        for application to the current matter.\n\nDo not rely on transferability without
        an applicable state rule, approval, or written regulator position.\n\nThe
        answer must be determined state by state and must cover more than technical
        change-of-control rules.\n\nThis path is possible only if Harbor remains the
        real provider and the relevant states permit the arrangement. The unified
        Mosaic account design may conflict with that position.\n\nThe result depends
        on the contracts and actual funds flow. Custody alone should not be treated
        as a licensing exemption or transfer mechanism.\n\nResearch saved. 4 sources
        retrieved; 0 with passages read.\n\nNext step: Identify the four Harbor-only
        states and complete one matrix covering license authority, transaction filings,
        interim operation, bank custody, outstanding obligations, and license surrender.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Detailed
        analysis</summary>\n\n**Practical answer**\n\n**Do not treat Harbor’s money
        transmitter licenses as assets that move to Mosaic in the asset purchase.**
        Use this closing rule:\n\n> **No confirmed authority means no regulated launch
        by Mosaic in that state.**\n\nThe asset purchase can still close. However,
        Mosaic should not activate regulated services in the four Harbor-only states
        unless one of these conditions is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its own license.\n2.
        The state approves a transfer or other license change.\n3. The regulator confirms
        a lawful interim structure.\n4. Harbor remains the real licensed provider
        under a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic blocks regulated functions in that
        state.\n\nThe planned unified Mosaic account is important. It suggests that
        Mosaic, not Harbor, will become the service provider. If that is correct,
        keeping Harbor’s legal entity and licenses alive might not give Mosaic authority
        to operate.\n\n**No verified operative authority retrieved.** The collection
        found the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act and a New York regulator
        licensing page. However, no exact provision about an asset sale, license transfer,
        interim operation, or custody was available for review. Also, a model act
        is not proof of the law adopted in a specific state. The state-specific conclusions
        below remain conditional.\n\n**Work needed before launch**\n\n| Work | Why
        | Proposed owner | Needed by | Evidence to proceed | Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n|
        Identify the four Harbor-only states | These states have the clearest authority
        gap | Licensing team | Now | Confirmed license list and covered activities
        | Block regulated functions in those states |\n| Build a matrix for every
        affected state | Transfer, notice, approval, and surrender rules can differ
        | State regulatory counsel | Before the closing conditions are final | Applicable
        rule, filing deadline, regulator response, and license status | Delay migration
        in the affected state |\n| Confirm the post-close service provider | The licensed
        entity must match the actual operating model | Product and deal counsel |
        Before customer notices and account design are final | Contracts, user interface,
        funds-flow diagram, and operating roles | Keep Harbor as the actual provider
        where permitted |\n| Review notices and approvals | An asset sale can create
        separate seller and buyer requirements | Licensing team | Before each state
        deadline | Filing receipts and required approvals or non-objections | Make
        approval a state launch condition |\n| Confirm interim operating authority
        | A pending application should not be assumed to permit operation | State
        regulatory counsel | Before close | Applicable rule or written regulator confirmation
        | Keep Harbor customers segregated or restrict transactions |\n| Review partner-bank
        arrangements | Bank custody does not, by itself, establish Mosaic’s licensing
        position | Payments counsel and bank relationship owner | Before balances
        move | Bank agreements, account titles, control rights, reconciliation design,
        and bank consent | Keep funds and obligations in the existing structure |\n|
        Prepare license run-off and surrender plans | Harbor may retain duties for
        balances, claims, records, and reports | Harbor compliance and deal counsel
        | Before surrender or operational shutdown | Regulator-approved plan and continued
        bonds and financial coverage | Keep Harbor licensed and operational longer
        |\n\n**State notice and approval**\n\nDo not search only for a rule called
        “license transfer.” Review each state for:\n\n- sale of substantially all
        assets;\n- change of control;\n- change in business plan;\n- change in licensed
        activities;\n- assignment of outstanding payment obligations;\n- change in
        responsible persons, locations, or agents;\n- license surrender or termination;\n-
        customer agreement assignment; and\n- movement of stored balances or customer
        funds.\n\nAn asset purchase might fall outside a technical “change of control”
        rule because Harbor’s ownership does not change. That does not resolve the
        issue. Harbor might still need a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic might
        separately need authority before it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe
        state matrix should distinguish:\n\n- notice only;\n- approval before closing;\n-
        approval before customer migration;\n- new license required;\n- operation
        permitted while an application is pending;\n- regulator-approved transition
        available; and\n- no supported interim path.\n\n**Interim operation**\n\nHarbor
        could remain the licensed provider for a transition period. However, the structure
        must be real, not only contractual language.\n\nA supportable structure would
        normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor remains responsible to customers.\n-
        Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n- Harbor controls the regulated
        activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses, bonds, and financial coverage
        remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding obligations remain covered.\n-
        Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints, and examinations.\n- Required
        records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational role is permitted.\n- The
        partner bank accepts the structure.\n- Each relevant regulator permits or
        accepts the structure.\n\nThe present plan creates tension with this approach.
        A single Mosaic account, one combined balance, and full access to Mosaic products
        make it harder to show that Harbor remains the true provider.\n\n**Partner-bank
        custody**\n\nA partner bank account is not automatically a substitute for
        a money transmitter license. The key questions concern the complete activity
        and obligation flow.\n\nFor each customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1.
        Who receives the customer’s instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to
        transmit or return the funds?\n3. In whose name is the bank account held?\n4.
        Is it a custodial or “for benefit of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6.
        Who owns the ledger and resolves errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer
        fails?\n8. Which entity owes the customer a refund?\n9. Which entity’s license,
        bond, and permissible investments cover the obligation?\n10. Does the bank
        agreement permit assignment, migration, or a change in the program manager?\n11.
        Is bank consent required before closing or migration?\n12. What happens to
        funds if Harbor, Mosaic, or the bank relationship ends?\n\nA bank-led model
        might provide a different licensing analysis if the bank is the actual provider
        and Mosaic performs only permitted services. A bank account that merely holds
        funds for Mosaic or Harbor is different. The legal documents, customer terms,
        control rights, and actual operations must all support the claimed model.\n\nAlso
        review:\n\n- account segregation;\n- daily reconciliation;\n- shortfalls and
        reserve funding;\n- bank setoff rights;\n- liens and security interests;\n-
        continuity if the account is frozen;\n- treatment of pending transfers;\n-
        return and chargeback duties;\n- insolvency treatment;\n- customer disclosures;
        and\n- whether any deposit-insurance statement is accurate for the actual
        account structure.\n\n**Recommended closing position**\n\nKeep the acquisition
        closing separate from the regulated-service launch.\n\nFor the four Harbor-only
        states, use a state launch hold unless Mosaic has documented authority. For
        overlapping states, confirm that Mosaic’s existing licenses cover the complete
        post-close product set and funds flow.\n\nDo not surrender Harbor’s licenses
        or release its bonds until the applicable regulators permit it and all outstanding
        obligations have been assigned, completed, or placed into an approved run-off
        structure.\n\nThis investigation does not change the current recommendation.
        It adds one material point: **partner-bank custody is part of the licensing
        analysis, but custody alone does not cure an authority gap.**\n\n</details>\n\nResearch
        history: [Saved research 1](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n\n</details>\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045
        -->\n### BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor's prior KYC (with missing
        underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay's independent
        CIP/AML obligations\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe current no-reverification
        plan is not ready for approval. Mosaic has not confirmed that its anti-money-laundering
        and customer identification program permits reliance on Harbor’s prior KYC.
        Pass/fail results alone may not provide the records or risk information that
        Mosaic needs.\n\nMosaic should not give an affected user unrestricted access
        unless compliance confirms that reliance is permitted and that the available
        records are sufficient, or a defined remediation process is complete.\n\n**Rule
        and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched. No saved authority establishes
        Mosaic’s precise federal duties or whether Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s checks
        after this asset purchase.\n\nThe unverified legal premise is that the entity
        providing the post-close financial service must follow its applicable customer
        identification, recordkeeping, risk-rating, and ongoing anti-money-laundering
        duties. The precise research question is whether Mosaic may adopt or rely
        on Harbor’s prior verification, and what records or remediation Mosaic must
        retain when the underlying identity documents are unavailable.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor
        verified the users through a vendor that closed in 2024. Mosaic has pass/fail
        results for all users but lacks the underlying documents for users onboarded
        before 2023. Mosaic’s compliance team has not confirmed whether its own program
        permits reliance.\n\nIf Mosaic’s program and applicable law permit reliance
        on Harbor’s process and retained results, Mosaic may be able to migrate some
        users without full reverification. Mosaic would still need evidence that the
        prior process, data, sanctions screening, risk rating, and records meet the
        applicable requirements.\n\nIf reliance is not permitted, or if the evidence
        is inadequate, Mosaic will need reverification or another approved remediation.
        Until then, it should restrict the affected accounts or delay their migration.
        This control does not resolve licensing, alert, or monitoring issues.\n\n**Next
        step**\n\nCompliance should document the applicable program rule, divide users
        into supported and unsupported groups, and define the evidence or reverification
        needed for each group. The result must support a clear migration rule for
        pre-2023 users.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:start
        -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38
        -->\n### SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor's
        ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe
        approximately 40 open alerts and recent SAR history require authorized review
        before Mosaic accepts the related users and activity without restrictions.
        The current record does not show whether the alerts are routine, overdue,
        linked to material misconduct, or relevant to the acquisition terms.\n\nA
        record gap does not prove a violation. However, unread alerts prevent Mosaic
        from assessing the risk it would take into its platform.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis
        issue has not been researched. No saved authority establishes who must resolve
        Harbor’s existing alerts, make any required filing, retain related records,
        or perform continuing review after an asset purchase.\n\nThe unverified legal
        premise is that the responsible regulated entity must assess potentially suspicious
        activity and meet applicable reporting and recordkeeping duties. The precise
        research question is how those duties are divided between Harbor and Mosaic
        for pre-close conduct, transferred accounts, and post-close continuing activity.\n\nAccess
        to SAR material can be legally restricted. Diligence must use authorized reviewers
        and approved access controls. This analysis does not direct Harbor to disclose
        or transfer restricted material to an unauthorized person.\n\n**Application**\n\nDiligence
        identified about 40 open alerts and “a handful” of SARs from the last year.
        None have been reviewed for this matter.\n\nOlder conduct may remain Harbor’s
        responsibility, while Mosaic may have duties for activity that continues after
        migration. The asset purchase documents can allocate work and cost between
        the parties, but contractual allocation may not change a regulator’s view
        of the responsible entity.\n\nIf the review finds overdue cases, connected
        accounts, control failures, or material undisclosed conduct, Mosaic may need
        account restrictions, remediation, revised closing protection, or a change
        to migration scope. If authorized review clears the cases and confirms proper
        handling, this obstacle becomes smaller but does not resolve KYC or monitoring
        continuity.\n\n**Next step**\n\nUse an authorized diligence team to triage
        the alerts and review permitted SAR-related information. Produce an aging
        and risk summary, assign each unresolved case to Harbor or Mosaic, and identify
        any effect on account migration or deal protection.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:start
        -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542
        -->\n### Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
        when the SaaS contract terminates at close\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic
        should validate the replacement transaction-monitoring feed before migrated
        users receive full access. Repointing the feed on day one without tested coverage
        creates a risk that transactions will not be captured, scored, or investigated
        correctly.\n\nIf validation is incomplete, the fallback should be continued
        Harbor coverage, a delayed migration, or transaction restrictions. The current
        record does not show that any fallback is available.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis
        issue has not been researched. No saved authority states the precise monitoring
        duty that applies to Harbor or Mosaic.\n\nThe unverified legal premise is
        that the responsible regulated provider must operate monitoring that is suitable
        for its risks and can support alert review and required reporting. The precise
        research question is which monitoring and continuity duties apply to each
        entity at close and during migration.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s third-party
        monitoring contract ends at close. The plan is to repoint Harbor’s transaction
        feed to Mosaic’s engine on day one.\n\nTechnical connectivity alone is not
        sufficient. Validation should establish complete data capture, correct field
        mapping, suitable scenarios and thresholds, timely alert creation, case ownership,
        historical-data availability, reconciliation, and recovery from failed feeds.\n\nThis
        work depends on the operating-provider and KYC decisions. Mosaic’s engine
        must monitor the actual products, customer risks, and funds flow that will
        exist after close. It must also support any continuing review of Harbor’s
        open cases.\n\n**Next step**\n\nComplete an end-to-end test using representative
        Harbor activity. The result needed to proceed is documented data completeness,
        alert generation, case routing, reconciliation, and a tested failure procedure.\n\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:start -->\nInitial analysis
        — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:end
        -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66 -->\n### Marketing compliance:
        the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money transmission or consumer protection
        implications\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe bonus should not launch at close+1
        until its operating terms and disclosures are reviewed. The offer is lower
        priority than licensing, KYC, alerts, and monitoring, but its planned timing
        leaves little room to correct unclear or misleading terms.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis
        issue has not been researched. No saved authority establishes the rules that
        apply to the proposed promotion.\n\nThe unverified legal premise is that the
        offer must accurately state its eligibility, required transfer, payment timing,
        limits, exclusions, expiration, and any right to reverse the bonus. Its funds
        flow must also fit the approved account and licensing structure. The precise
        research question is which state promotion, consumer-protection, money-transmission,
        unclaimed-property, tax, and disclosure rules apply to the final design.\n\n**Application**\n\nThe
        only reported terms are a $50 bonus on the first transfer and a planned close+1
        launch. The record does not state:\n\n- who qualifies;\n- the minimum or type
        of transfer;\n- who funds the bonus;\n- when it becomes available;\n- whether
        withdrawal or account-duration limits apply;\n- whether the offer is limited
        by state;\n- how disputes, reversals, fraud, and tax reporting are handled;
        or\n- what the customer-facing disclosures will say.\n\nThese terms determine
        whether the campaign is accurate and operationally supportable. The campaign
        must also exclude any state or user group whose migration or service access
        is held.\n\n**Next step**\n\nMarketing should provide the final offer mechanics,
        customer terms, creative material, state scope, and funds flow. Legal and
        compliance should approve that package before launch. If approval is not complete,
        delay the campaign without delaying otherwise lawful migration work.\n\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:start -->\nInitial analysis
        — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:end
        -->\n\n## Alternatives considered\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4
        -->\n### Bank-held funds timing test — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved
        alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
        this test only, a bank would hold the relevant funds while Mosaic controlled
        transfer instructions. The arrangement would depend on contract completion
        and bank operating setup. The test uses a November 15, 2026 migration and
        December 3, 2026 bank readiness date. It also assumes missing pre-2023 identity
        documents, 40 pending alert cases, and monitoring that ends at close.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nBank
        custody could change part of the licensing and safeguarding analysis if the
        contracts, customer terms, control rights, and actual operations support a
        bank-led model.\n\n**Trade-offs and added risks**\n\nOn the test dates, bank
        integration would be ready 18 days after the assumed migration date. The option
        therefore makes the tested November 15 launch harder unless readiness moves
        earlier or migration moves later.\n\nMosaic would still control transfer instructions.
        Bank custody alone does not establish that the bank is the regulated service
        provider or that Mosaic may operate without its own authority.\n\n**Issues
        that remain**\n\nThe option does not resolve missing KYC documents, pending
        alerts, SAR handling, or replacement monitoring. It also depends on completed
        bank contracts and operating setup.\n\n**Next action**\n\nThe saved working
        note names Mara Chen to obtain a dated bank-readiness plan and confirm whether
        the bank can support November 15. This is saved scenario guidance, not an
        assignment or commitment. The note also calls for assigned plans covering
        identity records, alerts, and monitoring.\n\nUse this option only if the bank
        model is legally supportable and can be operational before the chosen migration
        date. Otherwise, use it as a later transition structure rather than a basis
        for the initial launch.\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6 -->\n###
        Bank-held funds structure — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
        this hypothetical only, a partner bank holds customer funds.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nThe
        model could reduce part of Mosaic’s direct funds-custody role. It could support
        a different licensing analysis if the bank is the actual provider and Mosaic
        performs only permitted services.\n\n**Trade-offs and added risks**\n\nCustody
        alone does not resolve who conducts the regulated activity. The option adds
        dependency on bank agreements, consent, account setup, control rights, reconciliation,
        and operating readiness.\n\n**Issues that remain**\n\nThe following points
        remain open:\n\n- who contracts with users;\n- who controls transfer instructions
        and settlement;\n- who records balances and owes repayment;\n- how KYC, monitoring,
        alerts, SARs, privacy, and marketing duties are allocated; and\n- whether
        each affected state accepts the structure.\n\nThe option does not by itself
        resolve any KYC, alert, monitoring, or marketing issue.\n\n**Next action**\n\nPrepare
        the proposed customer, funds, instruction, settlement, ledger, loss, refund,
        and compliance flows. Compare them with the existing full day-one Mosaic model.
        Use the bank option only if those documents and actual operations establish
        a lawful bank-led structure and the bank can be ready on time.\n\n## Next
        actions\n\n1. **Resolve the state launch boundary.**  \n   **Deliverable:**
        A reconciled license list and state-by-state authority matrix.  \n   **Result
        needed:** Documented authority or an approved transition path for every planned
        post-close activity.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Day-one service activation
        and customer notices.  \n   **Fallback:** Hold regulated functions in any
        state without confirmed authority.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Licensing
        team with state regulatory counsel; start now and finish before closing conditions
        and launch scope are final.\n\n2. **Review the alerts and SAR history through
        authorized channels.**  \n   **Deliverable:** An aging, risk, ownership, and
        remediation summary.  \n   **Result needed:** Each open case has an authorized
        owner, required action, and migration treatment.  \n   **Dependent decision:**
        Which users can migrate without restrictions and whether deal protection must
        change.  \n   **Fallback:** Restrict affected accounts and preserve Harbor’s
        handling responsibilities where lawful.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:**
        Harbor and Mosaic anti-money-laundering leads with deal counsel; complete
        before migration approval.\n\n3. **Set the KYC migration rule.**  \n   **Deliverable:**
        A documented compliance position and user segmentation plan.  \n   **Result
        needed:** Evidence that reliance is permitted and records are sufficient,
        or a defined reverification process.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Migration
        of pre-2023 users without restrictions.  \n   **Fallback:** Reverify, restrict,
        or delay the affected accounts.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Mosaic
        compliance; complete before user migration rules and notices are final.\n\n4.
        **Validate transaction monitoring.**  \n   **Deliverable:** End-to-end test
        results and a continuity procedure.  \n   **Result needed:** Complete data
        capture, correct alert generation and routing, reconciliation, and tested
        recovery.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Full post-close transaction access.
        \ \n   **Fallback:** Extend Harbor coverage if available, delay migration,
        or impose transaction limits.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Mosaic
        anti-money-laundering operations and engineering; finish before Harbor’s monitoring
        contract ends at close.\n\n5. **Review the welcome bonus.**  \n   **Deliverable:**
        Approved mechanics, terms, disclosures, state scope, and funds flow.  \n   **Result
        needed:** An accurate and operationally supportable offer that matches launch
        restrictions.  \n   **Dependent activity:** The planned close+1 campaign.
        \ \n   **Fallback:** Delay or narrow the campaign.  \n   **Proposed owner
        and timing:** Marketing with consumer and payments counsel; complete after
        the permitted launch scope is known and before campaign release.\n\n## Current
        work product and supporting records\n\n- [Original request](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md)\n-
        [Reported facts](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md)\n- [Money transmission
