    available_excerpt: "# Harbor 2 matter dossier\n\n## Current position\n\nThe Harbor
      Pay migration needs legal and compliance review before the planned Nov 15 close.
      This is the accepted working view. No decision has been recorded.\n\nThis draft
      recommends continuing close preparation but making the day-one service migration
      conditional. Mosaic should not give all Harbor users full access until:\n\n1.
      Mosaic has documented authority for each post-close service in each affected
      state.\n2. Compliance confirms that Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s know-your-customer
      (KYC) results, or defines and completes remediation.\n3. Authorized reviewers
      assess Harbor’s open alerts and suspicious activity report (SAR) history.\n4.
      Mosaic tests the replacement transaction-monitoring feed and finds no material
      coverage gap.\n\nIf a condition is not met, Mosaic should hold the affected
      state launch, restrict affected accounts, or delay full product access. The
      $50 welcome bonus should also wait for review of its structure, terms, funding,
      and disclosures.\n\nThe saved material does not establish that the acquisition
      close itself must wait. However, the unread alerts and SAR history could affect
      deal terms, risk allocation, or the decision to close.\n\n### Assumptions used\n\n-
      Harbor is subject to the state money-transmission and federal anti-money-laundering
      requirements discussed below. The licensing, KYC, alert, and monitoring conclusions
      depend on this unverified legal premise.\n- Mosaic will become the operating
      provider when Harbor users receive a unified Mosaic account, combined balance,
      and access to Mosaic products. The licensing analysis depends on this inference.\n-
      The analysis does not assume that Harbor’s licenses transfer, that Harbor’s
      KYC results satisfy Mosaic’s program, or that the monitoring transition will
      work without a gap.\n\n### Record conflicts\n\n- Harbor reportedly has licenses
      in 38 states, Mosaic has licenses in 41 states, and the combined footprint is
      44 states. A 44-state footprint is three states larger than Mosaic’s 41-state
      footprint, but the record says the acquisition opens four new markets. The license
      lists and the intended meaning of “market” are needed. Until then, the states
      requiring separate authority cannot be identified reliably.\n- Matter metadata
      gives a target date of `2026-09-11`. The reported close is “Nov 15,” approximately
      ten weeks after the Sept. 9 intake. A saved hypothetical uses November 15, 2026,
      but that does not establish the actual closing year. The operative close date
      and year remain unresolved.\n\n## Decision question\n\nDoes any part of the
      Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal review before the Nov 15 close?\n\n##
      Issues\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045 -->\n### Money transmission
      licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under the combined 44-state footprint
      and whether Harbor's MTLs transfer/survive the acquisition\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic
      should not treat Harbor’s money transmitter licenses as assets that automatically
      move to Mosaic through the reported asset purchase. Mosaic should not start
      regulated services in a state unless it has documented authority for its complete
      post-close activity.\n\nThe acquisition close and the service launch can be
      managed as separate milestones. If authority is not established, the present
      fallback is to hold the affected state launch or restrict regulated functions.\n\n**Rule
      and support**\n\nSaved research concludes that the answer must be determined
      state by state. The review must cover Mosaic’s authority, transaction notices
      or approvals, interim operations, outstanding customer obligations, and Harbor’s
      license surrender.\n\nFour sources were retrieved, but no operative passage
      was selected, read, or verified. They do not establish the rule in any affected
      state:\n\n- [Money transmission research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
      [source:SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538]\n- [source:SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4]\n- [source:SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413]\n-
      [source:SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200]\n\nThe model act is not proof of any state’s
      adopted law. The premise that an asset purchase does not automatically give
      Mosaic Harbor’s operating authority remains an unverified state-law conclusion.\n\n**Application**\n\nMosaic
      plans to use or assume Harbor’s licenses in the new markets. The planned unified
      Mosaic account, combined balance, and access to Mosaic products indicate that
      Mosaic may become the actual provider. If so, keeping Harbor’s entity or licenses
      active might not authorize Mosaic’s conduct.\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed
      provider during a transition only if customer contracts, funds flow, operating
      control, licenses, bonds, records, and applicable state rules support that result.
      The documents and actual operations must match.\n\nA partner bank holding funds
      would not alone resolve the issue. The analysis still depends on who contracts
      with users, controls transfers, owes repayment, records balances, resolves errors,
      and performs regulated duties.\n\n**Next step**\n\nIdentify the Harbor-only
      jurisdictions and prepare a state matrix. For each state, determine Mosaic’s
      authority, required filings or approvals, operation while an application is
      pending, treatment of customer obligations, Harbor’s run-off duties, and the
      launch restriction needed if authority is not established.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:start
      -->\n<details>\n<summary>Saved research and prior analysis</summary>\n\nPreserved
      research snapshot. Its facts and assumptions may predate later records. Use
      the current answer above for application to the current matter.\n\nDo not rely
      on transferability without an applicable state rule, approval, or written regulator
      position.\n\nThe answer must be determined state by state and must cover more
      than technical change-of-control rules.\n\nThis path is possible only if Harbor
      remains the real provider and the relevant states permit the arrangement. The
      unified Mosaic account design may conflict with that position.\n\nThe result
      depends on the contracts and actual funds flow. Custody alone should not be
      treated as a licensing exemption or transfer mechanism.\n\nResearch saved. 4
      sources retrieved; 0 with passages read.\n\nNext step: Identify the four Harbor-only
      states and complete one matrix covering license authority, transaction filings,
      interim operation, bank custody, outstanding obligations, and license surrender.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Detailed
      analysis</summary>\n\n**Practical answer**\n\n**Do not treat Harbor’s money
      transmitter licenses as assets that move to Mosaic in the asset purchase.**
      Use this closing rule:\n\n> **No confirmed authority means no regulated launch
      by Mosaic in that state.**\n\nThe asset purchase can still close. However, Mosaic
      should not activate regulated services in the four Harbor-only states unless
      one of these conditions is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its own license.\n2. The
      state approves a transfer or other license change.\n3. The regulator confirms
      a lawful interim structure.\n4. Harbor remains the real licensed provider under
      a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic blocks regulated functions in that state.\n\nThe
      planned unified Mosaic account is important. It suggests that Mosaic, not Harbor,
      will become the service provider. If that is correct, keeping Harbor’s legal
      entity and licenses alive might not give Mosaic authority to operate.\n\n**No
      verified operative authority retrieved.** The collection found the CSBS Model
      Money Transmission Modernization Act and a New York regulator licensing page.
      However, no exact provision about an asset sale, license transfer, interim operation,
      or custody was available for review. Also, a model act is not proof of the law
      adopted in a specific state. The state-specific conclusions below remain conditional.\n\n**Work
      needed before launch**\n\n| Work | Why | Proposed owner | Needed by | Evidence
      to proceed | Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Identify the four Harbor-only
      states | These states have the clearest authority gap | Licensing team | Now
      | Confirmed license list and covered activities | Block regulated functions
      in those states |\n| Build a matrix for every affected state | Transfer, notice,
      approval, and surrender rules can differ | State regulatory counsel | Before
      the closing conditions are final | Applicable rule, filing deadline, regulator
      response, and license status | Delay migration in the affected state |\n| Confirm
      the post-close service provider | The licensed entity must match the actual
      operating model | Product and deal counsel | Before customer notices and account
      design are final | Contracts, user interface, funds-flow diagram, and operating
      roles | Keep Harbor as the actual provider where permitted |\n| Review notices
      and approvals | An asset sale can create separate seller and buyer requirements
      | Licensing team | Before each state deadline | Filing receipts and required
      approvals or non-objections | Make approval a state launch condition |\n| Confirm
      interim operating authority | A pending application should not be assumed to
      permit operation | State regulatory counsel | Before close | Applicable rule
      or written regulator confirmation | Keep Harbor customers segregated or restrict
      transactions |\n| Review partner-bank arrangements | Bank custody does not,
      by itself, establish Mosaic’s licensing position | Payments counsel and bank
      relationship owner | Before balances move | Bank agreements, account titles,
      control rights, reconciliation design, and bank consent | Keep funds and obligations
      in the existing structure |\n| Prepare license run-off and surrender plans |
      Harbor may retain duties for balances, claims, records, and reports | Harbor
      compliance and deal counsel | Before surrender or operational shutdown | Regulator-approved
      plan and continued bonds and financial coverage | Keep Harbor licensed and operational
      longer |\n\n**State notice and approval**\n\nDo not search only for a rule called
      “license transfer.” Review each state for:\n\n- sale of substantially all assets;\n-
      change of control;\n- change in business plan;\n- change in licensed activities;\n-
      assignment of outstanding payment obligations;\n- change in responsible persons,
      locations, or agents;\n- license surrender or termination;\n- customer agreement
      assignment; and\n- movement of stored balances or customer funds.\n\nAn asset
      purchase might fall outside a technical “change of control” rule because Harbor’s
      ownership does not change. That does not resolve the issue. Harbor might still
      need a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic might separately need authority
      before it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe state matrix should distinguish:\n\n-
      notice only;\n- approval before closing;\n- approval before customer migration;\n-
      new license required;\n- operation permitted while an application is pending;\n-
      regulator-approved transition available; and\n- no supported interim path.\n\n**Interim
      operation**\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider for a transition period.
      However, the structure must be real, not only contractual language.\n\nA supportable
      structure would normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor remains responsible
      to customers.\n- Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n- Harbor controls
      the regulated activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses, bonds, and financial
      coverage remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding obligations remain
      covered.\n- Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints, and examinations.\n-
      Required records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational role is permitted.\n-
      The partner bank accepts the structure.\n- Each relevant regulator permits or
      accepts the structure.\n\nThe present plan creates tension with this approach.
      A single Mosaic account, one combined balance, and full access to Mosaic products
      make it harder to show that Harbor remains the true provider.\n\n**Partner-bank
      custody**\n\nA partner bank account is not automatically a substitute for a
      money transmitter license. The key questions concern the complete activity and
      obligation flow.\n\nFor each customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1.
      Who receives the customer’s instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to transmit
      or return the funds?\n3. In whose name is the bank account held?\n4. Is it a
      custodial or “for benefit of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6. Who
      owns the ledger and resolves errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer fails?\n8.
      Which entity owes the customer a refund?\n9. Which entity’s license, bond, and
      permissible investments cover the obligation?\n10. Does the bank agreement permit
      assignment, migration, or a change in the program manager?\n11. Is bank consent
      required before closing or migration?\n12. What happens to funds if Harbor,
      Mosaic, or the bank relationship ends?\n\nA bank-led model might provide a different
      licensing analysis if the bank is the actual provider and Mosaic performs only
      permitted services. A bank account that merely holds funds for Mosaic or Harbor
      is different. The legal documents, customer terms, control rights, and actual
      operations must all support the claimed model.\n\nAlso review:\n\n- account
      segregation;\n- daily reconciliation;\n- shortfalls and reserve funding;\n-
      bank setoff rights;\n- liens and security interests;\n- continuity if the account
      is frozen;\n- treatment of pending transfers;\n- return and chargeback duties;\n-
      insolvency treatment;\n- customer disclosures; and\n- whether any deposit-insurance
      statement is accurate for the actual account structure.\n\n**Recommended closing
      position**\n\nKeep the acquisition closing separate from the regulated-service
      launch.\n\nFor the four Harbor-only states, use a state launch hold unless Mosaic
      has documented authority. For overlapping states, confirm that Mosaic’s existing
      licenses cover the complete post-close product set and funds flow.\n\nDo not
      surrender Harbor’s licenses or release its bonds until the applicable regulators
      permit it and all outstanding obligations have been assigned, completed, or
      placed into an approved run-off structure.\n\nThis investigation does not change
      the current recommendation. It adds one material point: **partner-bank custody
      is part of the licensing analysis, but custody alone does not cure an authority
      gap.**\n\n</details>\n\nResearch history: [Saved research 1](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n\n</details>\n<!--
      retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045
      -->\n### BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor's prior KYC (with missing
      underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay's independent
      CIP/AML obligations\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe saved material does not support
      a full day-one migration with no re-verification. Mosaic has not confirmed whether
      its anti-money-laundering and customer identification program permits reliance
      on Harbor’s prior KYC. The missing pre-2023 records may prevent Mosaic from
      showing that its own requirements are met.\n\nIf Mosaic’s program permits reliance
      and the retained evidence meets its requirements, targeted remediation may be
      sufficient. If it does not, affected users should be re-verified or restricted
      before receiving relevant services.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has
      not been researched. The unverified legal premise is that Mosaic must apply
      its own risk-based customer identification, recordkeeping, and anti-money-laundering
      controls when it becomes the service provider.\n\nThe precise research question
      is whether Mosaic may rely on identification work completed by Harbor, and what
      evidence, agreement, certification, or remediation is required when underlying
      documents are unavailable.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s former KYC vendor
      shut down in 2024. Mosaic has pass/fail results for all users, but it lacks
      underlying documents for users onboarded before 2023. A pass/fail result shows
      that a process produced an outcome. It does not establish which information
      was collected, how identity was verified, whether required records were retained,
      or whether Harbor’s process matches Mosaic’s program.\n\nThe affected population
      is not stated. That count matters because it affects whether remediation can
      finish before launch and whether restrictions can be targeted.\n\n**Next step**\n\nCompliance
      should compare Harbor’s KYC process and available records with Mosaic’s written
      program. The required output is a documented reliance or remediation decision,
      the affected user count, and account controls for users who do not meet the
      approved standard.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:start
      -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
      retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38
      -->\n### SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor's
      ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability\n\n**Current answer**\n\nAuthorized
      reviewers should assess the approximately 40 open alerts and the SAR history
      before Mosaic accepts unrestricted activity from the affected users. The saved
      facts do not establish that Mosaic inherits every Harbor duty, but the unread
      material could reveal reportable conduct, control failures, customer risk, or
      facts relevant to the acquisition.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has
      not been researched. The legal treatment may depend on which entity identified
      the conduct, when relevant deadlines began, which entity remains responsible
      after the asset purchase, what the purchase agreement assigns, and whether applicable
      law permits access to specific SAR material.\n\nSAR information is sensitive.
      Diligence must distinguish lawful access by authorized personnel from disclosure
      or transfer of restricted material. The precise research question is which entity
      must review, decide, file, retain, and continue monitoring each pre-close and
      post-close matter.\n\n**Application**\n\nDiligence identified approximately
      40 open alerts and “a handful” of SARs from the last year. None has been reviewed.
      The record does not identify the alert dates, subjects, conduct, status, prior
      decisions, or affected accounts.\n\nThis is more than a record gap. The unread
      material could change account migration controls and the deal’s risk allocation.
      It does not, by itself, prove a violation or successor liability.\n\n**Next
      step**\n\nUse authorized personnel to create a privileged case inventory. Classify
      each alert by age, subject, activity, deadline, disposition, required action,
      and affected account. Separately identify what SAR information Mosaic may lawfully
      review or receive. Escalate any material findings into migration controls and
      the deal review.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:start
      -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
      retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542
      -->\n### Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
      when the SaaS contract terminates at close\n\n**Current answer**\n\nA day-one
      feed change is not enough by itself. Mosaic should validate that its monitoring
      system receives complete and accurate Harbor data, applies suitable rules, produces
      alerts, and supports investigation without a material gap.\n\nIf validation
      is incomplete, Mosaic should extend the existing service if possible, limit
      migrated activity, or delay full product access.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis
      issue has not been researched. The conditional premise is that, if Mosaic and
      Harbor are subject to applicable anti-money-laundering duties, their monitoring
      controls must remain effective through the transition. A specific legal test
      and any applicable examination guidance have not been verified.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s
      monitoring contract terminates at close. The plan is to point Harbor’s transaction
      feed to Mosaic’s engine on day one. This creates a single transition point with
      no reported overlap period.\n\nThe saved record does not show field mapping,
      historical-data transfer, rule coverage, alert generation, reconciliation, access
      to old cases, failure handling, or test results. The open Harbor alerts also
      create a dependency: a new feed does not resolve existing cases.\n\n**Next step**\n\nComplete
      an end-to-end test before unrestricted launch. The evidence should include data
      reconciliation, rule and scenario coverage, sample alert results, historical
      access, case ownership, failure procedures, and an approved rollback or restriction
      plan.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:start -->\nInitial
      analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:end
      -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66 -->\n### Marketing compliance:
      the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money transmission or consumer protection
      implications\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe $50 welcome campaign should not launch
      at close+1 until its structure and disclosures are reviewed. The offer is lower
      priority than licensing, KYC, alerts, and monitoring, but it could create misleading
      claims or operational obligations if customers cannot use the promoted transfer
      service in every advertised state.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has
      not been researched. The applicable analysis may depend on consumer-protection
      rules, state promotional requirements, the funds flow, and the terms governing
      the bonus. No saved authority establishes that the bonus is a deposit, interest
      payment, or regulated transfer product.\n\nThe precise research question is
      whether the final offer structure requires specific terms, disclosures, eligibility
      limits, licensing coverage, or treatment of the bonus funds.\n\n**Application**\n\nThe
      only settled details are a $50 bonus on the first transfer and a proposed launch
      at close+1. The record does not state who funds the bonus, which users qualify,
      the required transfer amount, payment timing, expiration, exclusions, reversal
      rights, tax treatment, or how restrictions will be disclosed.\n\nThe campaign
      also depends on the other workstreams. Mosaic should not advertise immediate
      access in a state or to a user group whose migration remains restricted.\n\n**Next
      step**\n\nMarketing should provide the final offer terms, user journey, target
      jurisdictions, funding flow, and draft claims. Legal review should then confirm
      that the disclosures match actual eligibility, service availability, payment
      timing, and account restrictions.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:start
      -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
      retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:end -->\n\n## Alternatives considered\n\n<!--
      alternative:SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4 -->\n### Bank-held funds timing test
      — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
      this test only, a bank holds the relevant funds while Mosaic controls transfer
      instructions. The model depends on completion of the bank contract and operating
      setup. It assumes migration on November 15, 2026, and bank readiness on December
      3, 2026. It also assumes missing pre-2023 identity documents, 40 pending alerts,
      and monitoring ending at close.\n\n**Effect on the objective**\n\nThe option
      may change the funds-custody analysis. It does not establish that Mosaic can
      perform the regulated activity without its own authority.\n\nOn the hypothetical
      dates, it makes a November 15 migration harder because bank readiness is December
      3, 18 days later.\n\n**Added risks**\n\nThe option adds contract and integration
      dependencies. If the bank cannot complete its agreement and setup by migration,
      the structure is not operational.\n\n**Issues left unresolved**\n\nBank custody
      does not resolve missing identity records, pending alerts, SAR handling, or
      the monitoring transition. It also does not answer who contracts with users,
      controls transfers, owes repayment, and performs regulated duties.\n\n**Next
      action**\n\nThe saved working note proposes that Mara Chen obtain a dated bank-readiness
      plan and confirm whether the bank can support November 15. This is part of the
      hypothetical note, not a recorded assignment or decision. Use this option only
      if the bank structure is legally supportable and ready before the actual migration
      date.\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6 -->\n### Bank-held funds
      structure — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
      this test only, a partner bank holds customer funds.\n\n**Effect on the objective**\n\nA
      bank-held model could support a different licensing analysis if the bank is
      the actual provider and Mosaic performs only permitted services. Mere custody
      does not establish that result.\n\n**Added risks**\n\nThe structure requires
      clear contracts, control rights, bank consent, funds-flow design, customer terms,
      reconciliation, and operating responsibility. It could add implementation time
      without solving the launch conditions.\n\n**Issues left unresolved**\n\nThe
      alternative leaves open who contracts with users, controls transfer instructions
      and settlement, records balances, owes repayment, and handles KYC, monitoring,
      alerts, SARs, privacy, and marketing. It does not resolve those issues merely
      by moving the funds.\n\n**Next action**\n\nPrepare the proposed contracts, customer
      terms, funds-flow diagram, and operating roles. Compare them with the state
      licensing matrix. Use this structure only where the documents, actual operations,
      bank approval, and applicable state rules support it.\n\n## Next actions\n\n1.
      **Licensing authority matrix.**  \n   **Proposed owner:** State regulatory counsel
      with the licensing team.  \n   **Timing:** Before closing conditions, customer
      notices, and account design are final.  \n   **Result needed:** A verified list
      of affected states and documented authority, filing requirements, interim options,
      and launch restrictions.  \n   **Dependent activity:** State-by-state migration
      and access to Mosaic products.  \n   **Fallback:** Hold regulated functions
      in any state without documented authority.\n\n2. **Alert and SAR diligence review.**
      \ \n   **Proposed owner:** Authorized anti-money-laundering compliance reviewers
      with deal counsel.  \n   **Timing:** Before the close decision and before affected
      accounts receive unrestricted access.  \n   **Result needed:** A case inventory,
      required actions, lawful information-access plan, and identification of any
      deal or migration impact.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Deal risk allocation
      and account migration.  \n   **Fallback:** Restrict affected accounts and preserve
      Harbor’s case-handling capacity while issues remain open.\n\n3. **KYC reliance
      and remediation decision.**  \n   **Proposed owner:** Mosaic compliance.  \n
      \  **Timing:** Before migrated users receive full product access.  \n   **Result
      needed:** Written confirmation that reliance is permitted and adequately supported,
      or a remediation plan with the affected user count.  \n   **Dependent activity:**
      Migration without re-verification.  \n   **Fallback:** Re-verify or restrict
      users who do not meet the approved standard.\n\n4. **Monitoring transition validation.**
      \ \n   **Proposed owner:** Mosaic compliance and monitoring operations.  \n
      \  **Timing:** Before Harbor’s monitoring service ends or migrated transactions
      begin.  \n   **Result needed:** Successful end-to-end testing, reconciliation,
      historical access, case ownership, and rollback controls.  \n   **Dependent
      activity:** Unrestricted transaction activity after close.  \n   **Fallback:**
      Extend the existing service if possible, restrict activity, or delay full access.\n\n5.
      **Welcome bonus review.**  \n   **Proposed owner:** Marketing counsel with product
      and compliance teams.  \n   **Timing:** Before campaign approval and after launch
      restrictions are known.  \n   **Result needed:** Final terms and disclosures
      that match the actual funds flow, eligibility, state availability, and payment
      process.  \n   **Dependent activity:** The planned close+1 campaign.  \n   **Fallback:**
      Delay or narrow the campaign.\n\n## Current work product and supporting records\n\n-
      [Known facts](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md)\n- [Original request](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md)\n-
      [Money transmission research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
      [Completed intake work item](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/work-items/WI-20260909-dc797b.md)\n-
      [Prior dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-e1dcd612539ad45c6d6f.md)\n\n[Open
      saved dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-eecf5c02c431c10638ea.md)\n\nDossier
      generated and saved."

      message_id: MSG-20260912-cbe66a
      role: assistant
      content: "# Harbor 2 matter dossier\n\n## Current position\n\nThe Harbor Pay
        migration needs legal and compliance review before the planned Nov 15 close.
        This is the accepted working view. No decision has been recorded.\n\nThis
        draft recommends continuing close preparation but making the day-one service
        migration conditional. Mosaic should not give all Harbor users full access
        until:\n\n1. Mosaic has documented authority for each post-close service in
        each affected state.\n2. Compliance confirms that Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s
        know-your-customer (KYC) results, or defines and completes remediation.\n3.
        Authorized reviewers assess Harbor’s open alerts and suspicious activity report
        (SAR) history.\n4. Mosaic tests the replacement transaction-monitoring feed
        and finds no material coverage gap.\n\nIf a condition is not met, Mosaic should
        hold the affected state launch, restrict affected accounts, or delay full
        product access. The $50 welcome bonus should also wait for review of its structure,
        terms, funding, and disclosures.\n\nThe saved material does not establish
        that the acquisition close itself must wait. However, the unread alerts and
        SAR history could affect deal terms, risk allocation, or the decision to close.\n\n###
        Assumptions used\n\n- Harbor is subject to the state money-transmission and
        federal anti-money-laundering requirements discussed below. The licensing,
        KYC, alert, and monitoring conclusions depend on this unverified legal premise.\n-
        Mosaic will become the operating provider when Harbor users receive a unified
        Mosaic account, combined balance, and access to Mosaic products. The licensing
        analysis depends on this inference.\n- The analysis does not assume that Harbor’s
        licenses transfer, that Harbor’s KYC results satisfy Mosaic’s program, or
        that the monitoring transition will work without a gap.\n\n### Record conflicts\n\n-
        Harbor reportedly has licenses in 38 states, Mosaic has licenses in 41 states,
        and the combined footprint is 44 states. A 44-state footprint is three states
        larger than Mosaic’s 41-state footprint, but the record says the acquisition
        opens four new markets. The license lists and the intended meaning of “market”
        are needed. Until then, the states requiring separate authority cannot be
        identified reliably.\n- Matter metadata gives a target date of `2026-09-11`.
        The reported close is “Nov 15,” approximately ten weeks after the Sept. 9
        intake. A saved hypothetical uses November 15, 2026, but that does not establish
        the actual closing year. The operative close date and year remain unresolved.\n\n##
        Decision question\n\nDoes any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration
        need legal review before the Nov 15 close?\n\n## Issues\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045
        -->\n### Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate under
        the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor's MTLs transfer/survive
        the acquisition\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic should not treat Harbor’s
        money transmitter licenses as assets that automatically move to Mosaic through
        the reported asset purchase. Mosaic should not start regulated services in
        a state unless it has documented authority for its complete post-close activity.\n\nThe
        acquisition close and the service launch can be managed as separate milestones.
        If authority is not established, the present fallback is to hold the affected
        state launch or restrict regulated functions.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nSaved
        research concludes that the answer must be determined state by state. The
        review must cover Mosaic’s authority, transaction notices or approvals, interim
        operations, outstanding customer obligations, and Harbor’s license surrender.\n\nFour
        sources were retrieved, but no operative passage was selected, read, or verified.
        They do not establish the rule in any affected state:\n\n- [Money transmission
        research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
        [source:SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538]\n- [source:SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4]\n-
        [source:SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413]\n- [source:SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200]\n\nThe
        model act is not proof of any state’s adopted law. The premise that an asset
        purchase does not automatically give Mosaic Harbor’s operating authority remains
        an unverified state-law conclusion.\n\n**Application**\n\nMosaic plans to
        use or assume Harbor’s licenses in the new markets. The planned unified Mosaic
        account, combined balance, and access to Mosaic products indicate that Mosaic
        may become the actual provider. If so, keeping Harbor’s entity or licenses
        active might not authorize Mosaic’s conduct.\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed
        provider during a transition only if customer contracts, funds flow, operating
        control, licenses, bonds, records, and applicable state rules support that
        result. The documents and actual operations must match.\n\nA partner bank
        holding funds would not alone resolve the issue. The analysis still depends
        on who contracts with users, controls transfers, owes repayment, records balances,
        resolves errors, and performs regulated duties.\n\n**Next step**\n\nIdentify
        the Harbor-only jurisdictions and prepare a state matrix. For each state,
        determine Mosaic’s authority, required filings or approvals, operation while
        an application is pending, treatment of customer obligations, Harbor’s run-off
        duties, and the launch restriction needed if authority is not established.\n\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:start -->\n<details>\n<summary>Saved
        research and prior analysis</summary>\n\nPreserved research snapshot. Its
        facts and assumptions may predate later records. Use the current answer above
        for application to the current matter.\n\nDo not rely on transferability without
        an applicable state rule, approval, or written regulator position.\n\nThe
        answer must be determined state by state and must cover more than technical
        change-of-control rules.\n\nThis path is possible only if Harbor remains the
        real provider and the relevant states permit the arrangement. The unified
        Mosaic account design may conflict with that position.\n\nThe result depends
        on the contracts and actual funds flow. Custody alone should not be treated
        as a licensing exemption or transfer mechanism.\n\nResearch saved. 4 sources
        retrieved; 0 with passages read.\n\nNext step: Identify the four Harbor-only
        states and complete one matrix covering license authority, transaction filings,
        interim operation, bank custody, outstanding obligations, and license surrender.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Detailed
        analysis</summary>\n\n**Practical answer**\n\n**Do not treat Harbor’s money
        transmitter licenses as assets that move to Mosaic in the asset purchase.**
        Use this closing rule:\n\n> **No confirmed authority means no regulated launch
        by Mosaic in that state.**\n\nThe asset purchase can still close. However,
        Mosaic should not activate regulated services in the four Harbor-only states
        unless one of these conditions is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its own license.\n2.
        The state approves a transfer or other license change.\n3. The regulator confirms
        a lawful interim structure.\n4. Harbor remains the real licensed provider
        under a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic blocks regulated functions in that
        state.\n\nThe planned unified Mosaic account is important. It suggests that
        Mosaic, not Harbor, will become the service provider. If that is correct,
        keeping Harbor’s legal entity and licenses alive might not give Mosaic authority
        to operate.\n\n**No verified operative authority retrieved.** The collection
        found the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act and a New York regulator
        licensing page. However, no exact provision about an asset sale, license transfer,
        interim operation, or custody was available for review. Also, a model act
        is not proof of the law adopted in a specific state. The state-specific conclusions
        below remain conditional.\n\n**Work needed before launch**\n\n| Work | Why
        | Proposed owner | Needed by | Evidence to proceed | Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n|
        Identify the four Harbor-only states | These states have the clearest authority
        gap | Licensing team | Now | Confirmed license list and covered activities
        | Block regulated functions in those states |\n| Build a matrix for every
        affected state | Transfer, notice, approval, and surrender rules can differ
        | State regulatory counsel | Before the closing conditions are final | Applicable
        rule, filing deadline, regulator response, and license status | Delay migration
        in the affected state |\n| Confirm the post-close service provider | The licensed
        entity must match the actual operating model | Product and deal counsel |
        Before customer notices and account design are final | Contracts, user interface,
        funds-flow diagram, and operating roles | Keep Harbor as the actual provider
        where permitted |\n| Review notices and approvals | An asset sale can create
        separate seller and buyer requirements | Licensing team | Before each state
        deadline | Filing receipts and required approvals or non-objections | Make
        approval a state launch condition |\n| Confirm interim operating authority
        | A pending application should not be assumed to permit operation | State
        regulatory counsel | Before close | Applicable rule or written regulator confirmation
        | Keep Harbor customers segregated or restrict transactions |\n| Review partner-bank
        arrangements | Bank custody does not, by itself, establish Mosaic’s licensing
        position | Payments counsel and bank relationship owner | Before balances
        move | Bank agreements, account titles, control rights, reconciliation design,
        and bank consent | Keep funds and obligations in the existing structure |\n|
        Prepare license run-off and surrender plans | Harbor may retain duties for
        balances, claims, records, and reports | Harbor compliance and deal counsel
        | Before surrender or operational shutdown | Regulator-approved plan and continued
        bonds and financial coverage | Keep Harbor licensed and operational longer
        |\n\n**State notice and approval**\n\nDo not search only for a rule called
        “license transfer.” Review each state for:\n\n- sale of substantially all
        assets;\n- change of control;\n- change in business plan;\n- change in licensed
        activities;\n- assignment of outstanding payment obligations;\n- change in
        responsible persons, locations, or agents;\n- license surrender or termination;\n-
        customer agreement assignment; and\n- movement of stored balances or customer
        funds.\n\nAn asset purchase might fall outside a technical “change of control”
        rule because Harbor’s ownership does not change. That does not resolve the
        issue. Harbor might still need a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic might
        separately need authority before it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe
        state matrix should distinguish:\n\n- notice only;\n- approval before closing;\n-
        approval before customer migration;\n- new license required;\n- operation
        permitted while an application is pending;\n- regulator-approved transition
        available; and\n- no supported interim path.\n\n**Interim operation**\n\nHarbor
        could remain the licensed provider for a transition period. However, the structure
        must be real, not only contractual language.\n\nA supportable structure would
        normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor remains responsible to customers.\n-
        Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n- Harbor controls the regulated
        activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses, bonds, and financial coverage
        remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding obligations remain covered.\n-
        Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints, and examinations.\n- Required
        records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational role is permitted.\n- The
        partner bank accepts the structure.\n- Each relevant regulator permits or
        accepts the structure.\n\nThe present plan creates tension with this approach.
        A single Mosaic account, one combined balance, and full access to Mosaic products
        make it harder to show that Harbor remains the true provider.\n\n**Partner-bank
        custody**\n\nA partner bank account is not automatically a substitute for
        a money transmitter license. The key questions concern the complete activity
        and obligation flow.\n\nFor each customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1.
        Who receives the customer’s instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to
        transmit or return the funds?\n3. In whose name is the bank account held?\n4.
        Is it a custodial or “for benefit of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6.
        Who owns the ledger and resolves errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer
        fails?\n8. Which entity owes the customer a refund?\n9. Which entity’s license,
        bond, and permissible investments cover the obligation?\n10. Does the bank
        agreement permit assignment, migration, or a change in the program manager?\n11.
        Is bank consent required before closing or migration?\n12. What happens to
        funds if Harbor, Mosaic, or the bank relationship ends?\n\nA bank-led model
        might provide a different licensing analysis if the bank is the actual provider
        and Mosaic performs only permitted services. A bank account that merely holds
        funds for Mosaic or Harbor is different. The legal documents, customer terms,
        control rights, and actual operations must all support the claimed model.\n\nAlso
        review:\n\n- account segregation;\n- daily reconciliation;\n- shortfalls and
        reserve funding;\n- bank setoff rights;\n- liens and security interests;\n-
        continuity if the account is frozen;\n- treatment of pending transfers;\n-
        return and chargeback duties;\n- insolvency treatment;\n- customer disclosures;
        and\n- whether any deposit-insurance statement is accurate for the actual
        account structure.\n\n**Recommended closing position**\n\nKeep the acquisition
        closing separate from the regulated-service launch.\n\nFor the four Harbor-only
        states, use a state launch hold unless Mosaic has documented authority. For
        overlapping states, confirm that Mosaic’s existing licenses cover the complete
        post-close product set and funds flow.\n\nDo not surrender Harbor’s licenses
        or release its bonds until the applicable regulators permit it and all outstanding
        obligations have been assigned, completed, or placed into an approved run-off
        structure.\n\nThis investigation does not change the current recommendation.
        It adds one material point: **partner-bank custody is part of the licensing
        analysis, but custody alone does not cure an authority gap.**\n\n</details>\n\nResearch
        history: [Saved research 1](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n\n</details>\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045
        -->\n### BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor's prior KYC (with missing
        underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay's independent
        CIP/AML obligations\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe saved material does not support
        a full day-one migration with no re-verification. Mosaic has not confirmed
        whether its anti-money-laundering and customer identification program permits
        reliance on Harbor’s prior KYC. The missing pre-2023 records may prevent Mosaic
        from showing that its own requirements are met.\n\nIf Mosaic’s program permits
        reliance and the retained evidence meets its requirements, targeted remediation
        may be sufficient. If it does not, affected users should be re-verified or
        restricted before receiving relevant services.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis
        issue has not been researched. The unverified legal premise is that Mosaic
        must apply its own risk-based customer identification, recordkeeping, and
        anti-money-laundering controls when it becomes the service provider.\n\nThe
        precise research question is whether Mosaic may rely on identification work
        completed by Harbor, and what evidence, agreement, certification, or remediation
        is required when underlying documents are unavailable.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s
        former KYC vendor shut down in 2024. Mosaic has pass/fail results for all
        users, but it lacks underlying documents for users onboarded before 2023.
        A pass/fail result shows that a process produced an outcome. It does not establish
        which information was collected, how identity was verified, whether required
        records were retained, or whether Harbor’s process matches Mosaic’s program.\n\nThe
        affected population is not stated. That count matters because it affects whether
        remediation can finish before launch and whether restrictions can be targeted.\n\n**Next
        step**\n\nCompliance should compare Harbor’s KYC process and available records
        with Mosaic’s written program. The required output is a documented reliance
        or remediation decision, the affected user count, and account controls for
        users who do not meet the approved standard.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:start
        -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38
        -->\n### SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage Harbor's
        ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability\n\n**Current answer**\n\nAuthorized
        reviewers should assess the approximately 40 open alerts and the SAR history
        before Mosaic accepts unrestricted activity from the affected users. The saved
        facts do not establish that Mosaic inherits every Harbor duty, but the unread
        material could reveal reportable conduct, control failures, customer risk,
        or facts relevant to the acquisition.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue
        has not been researched. The legal treatment may depend on which entity identified
        the conduct, when relevant deadlines began, which entity remains responsible
        after the asset purchase, what the purchase agreement assigns, and whether
        applicable law permits access to specific SAR material.\n\nSAR information
        is sensitive. Diligence must distinguish lawful access by authorized personnel
        from disclosure or transfer of restricted material. The precise research question
        is which entity must review, decide, file, retain, and continue monitoring
        each pre-close and post-close matter.\n\n**Application**\n\nDiligence identified
        approximately 40 open alerts and “a handful” of SARs from the last year. None
        has been reviewed. The record does not identify the alert dates, subjects,
        conduct, status, prior decisions, or affected accounts.\n\nThis is more than
        a record gap. The unread material could change account migration controls
        and the deal’s risk allocation. It does not, by itself, prove a violation
        or successor liability.\n\n**Next step**\n\nUse authorized personnel to create
        a privileged case inventory. Classify each alert by age, subject, activity,
        deadline, disposition, required action, and affected account. Separately identify
        what SAR information Mosaic may lawfully review or receive. Escalate any material
        findings into migration controls and the deal review.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:start
        -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542
        -->\n### Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
        when the SaaS contract terminates at close\n\n**Current answer**\n\nA day-one
        feed change is not enough by itself. Mosaic should validate that its monitoring
        system receives complete and accurate Harbor data, applies suitable rules,
        produces alerts, and supports investigation without a material gap.\n\nIf
        validation is incomplete, Mosaic should extend the existing service if possible,
        limit migrated activity, or delay full product access.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis
        issue has not been researched. The conditional premise is that, if Mosaic
        and Harbor are subject to applicable anti-money-laundering duties, their monitoring
        controls must remain effective through the transition. A specific legal test
        and any applicable examination guidance have not been verified.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s
        monitoring contract terminates at close. The plan is to point Harbor’s transaction
        feed to Mosaic’s engine on day one. This creates a single transition point
        with no reported overlap period.\n\nThe saved record does not show field mapping,
        historical-data transfer, rule coverage, alert generation, reconciliation,
        access to old cases, failure handling, or test results. The open Harbor alerts
        also create a dependency: a new feed does not resolve existing cases.\n\n**Next
        step**\n\nComplete an end-to-end test before unrestricted launch. The evidence
        should include data reconciliation, rule and scenario coverage, sample alert
        results, historical access, case ownership, failure procedures, and an approved
        rollback or restriction plan.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:start
        -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66
        -->\n### Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state money
        transmission or consumer protection implications\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe
        $50 welcome campaign should not launch at close+1 until its structure and
        disclosures are reviewed. The offer is lower priority than licensing, KYC,
        alerts, and monitoring, but it could create misleading claims or operational
        obligations if customers cannot use the promoted transfer service in every
        advertised state.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched.
        The applicable analysis may depend on consumer-protection rules, state promotional
        requirements, the funds flow, and the terms governing the bonus. No saved
        authority establishes that the bonus is a deposit, interest payment, or regulated
        transfer product.\n\nThe precise research question is whether the final offer
        structure requires specific terms, disclosures, eligibility limits, licensing
        coverage, or treatment of the bonus funds.\n\n**Application**\n\nThe only
        settled details are a $50 bonus on the first transfer and a proposed launch
        at close+1. The record does not state who funds the bonus, which users qualify,
        the required transfer amount, payment timing, expiration, exclusions, reversal
        rights, tax treatment, or how restrictions will be disclosed.\n\nThe campaign
        also depends on the other workstreams. Mosaic should not advertise immediate
        access in a state or to a user group whose migration remains restricted.\n\n**Next
        step**\n\nMarketing should provide the final offer terms, user journey, target
        jurisdictions, funding flow, and draft claims. Legal review should then confirm
        that the disclosures match actual eligibility, service availability, payment
        timing, and account restrictions.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:start
        -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
        retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:end -->\n\n## Alternatives
        considered\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4 -->\n### Bank-held
        funds timing test — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
        this test only, a bank holds the relevant funds while Mosaic controls transfer
        instructions. The model depends on completion of the bank contract and operating
        setup. It assumes migration on November 15, 2026, and bank readiness on December
        3, 2026. It also assumes missing pre-2023 identity documents, 40 pending alerts,
        and monitoring ending at close.\n\n**Effect on the objective**\n\nThe option
        may change the funds-custody analysis. It does not establish that Mosaic can
        perform the regulated activity without its own authority.\n\nOn the hypothetical
        dates, it makes a November 15 migration harder because bank readiness is December
        3, 18 days later.\n\n**Added risks**\n\nThe option adds contract and integration
        dependencies. If the bank cannot complete its agreement and setup by migration,
        the structure is not operational.\n\n**Issues left unresolved**\n\nBank custody
        does not resolve missing identity records, pending alerts, SAR handling, or
        the monitoring transition. It also does not answer who contracts with users,
        controls transfers, owes repayment, and performs regulated duties.\n\n**Next
        action**\n\nThe saved working note proposes that Mara Chen obtain a dated
        bank-readiness plan and confirm whether the bank can support November 15.
        This is part of the hypothetical note, not a recorded assignment or decision.
        Use this option only if the bank structure is legally supportable and ready
        before the actual migration date.\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6
        -->\n### Bank-held funds structure — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved
        alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
        this test only, a partner bank holds customer funds.\n\n**Effect on the objective**\n\nA
        bank-held model could support a different licensing analysis if the bank is
        the actual provider and Mosaic performs only permitted services. Mere custody
        does not establish that result.\n\n**Added risks**\n\nThe structure requires
        clear contracts, control rights, bank consent, funds-flow design, customer
        terms, reconciliation, and operating responsibility. It could add implementation
        time without solving the launch conditions.\n\n**Issues left unresolved**\n\nThe
        alternative leaves open who contracts with users, controls transfer instructions
        and settlement, records balances, owes repayment, and handles KYC, monitoring,
        alerts, SARs, privacy, and marketing. It does not resolve those issues merely
        by moving the funds.\n\n**Next action**\n\nPrepare the proposed contracts,
        customer terms, funds-flow diagram, and operating roles. Compare them with
        the state licensing matrix. Use this structure only where the documents, actual
        operations, bank approval, and applicable state rules support it.\n\n## Next
        actions\n\n1. **Licensing authority matrix.**  \n   **Proposed owner:** State
        regulatory counsel with the licensing team.  \n   **Timing:** Before closing
        conditions, customer notices, and account design are final.  \n   **Result
        needed:** A verified list of affected states and documented authority, filing
        requirements, interim options, and launch restrictions.  \n   **Dependent
        activity:** State-by-state migration and access to Mosaic products.  \n   **Fallback:**
        Hold regulated functions in any state without documented authority.\n\n2.
        **Alert and SAR diligence review.**  \n   **Proposed owner:** Authorized anti-money-laundering
        compliance reviewers with deal counsel.  \n   **Timing:** Before the close
        decision and before affected accounts receive unrestricted access.  \n   **Result
        needed:** A case inventory, required actions, lawful information-access plan,
        and identification of any deal or migration impact.  \n   **Dependent activity:**
        Deal risk allocation and account migration.  \n   **Fallback:** Restrict affected
        accounts and preserve Harbor’s case-handling capacity while issues remain
        open.\n\n3. **KYC reliance and remediation decision.**  \n   **Proposed owner:**
        Mosaic compliance.  \n   **Timing:** Before migrated users receive full product
        access.  \n   **Result needed:** Written confirmation that reliance is permitted
        and adequately supported, or a remediation plan with the affected user count.
        \ \n   **Dependent activity:** Migration without re-verification.  \n   **Fallback:**
        Re-verify or restrict users who do not meet the approved standard.\n\n4. **Monitoring
        transition validation.**  \n   **Proposed owner:** Mosaic compliance and monitoring
        operations.  \n   **Timing:** Before Harbor’s monitoring service ends or migrated
        transactions begin.  \n   **Result needed:** Successful end-to-end testing,
        reconciliation, historical access, case ownership, and rollback controls.
        \ \n   **Dependent activity:** Unrestricted transaction activity after close.
        \ \n   **Fallback:** Extend the existing service if possible, restrict activity,
        or delay full access.\n\n5. **Welcome bonus review.**  \n   **Proposed owner:**
        Marketing counsel with product and compliance teams.  \n   **Timing:** Before
        campaign approval and after launch restrictions are known.  \n   **Result
        needed:** Final terms and disclosures that match the actual funds flow, eligibility,
        state availability, and payment process.  \n   **Dependent activity:** The
        planned close+1 campaign.  \n   **Fallback:** Delay or narrow the campaign.\n\n##
        Current work product and supporting records\n\n- [Known facts](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md)\n-
        [Original request](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md)\n- [Money transmission
        research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
        [Completed intake work item](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/work-items/WI-20260909-dc797b.md)\n-
        [Prior dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-e1dcd612539ad45c6d6f.md)\n\n[Open
        saved dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-eecf5c02c431c10638ea.md)\n\nDossier
        generated and saved."

    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/conversations/CONV-20260909-5299cf.md
    available_excerpt: '## Harbor 2 — preparation note (close targeted Nov 15)


      **Controlling question:** does any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration
      need legal review before the Nov 15 close? The newest turn ("Generate the Dossier")
      and the surrounding bank-held-funds comparisons are supporting work; they do
      not change that question. The record contains **no recorded decisions** at all,
      all five registered issues are `open`, and one intake question — how the $50
      bonus is structured — was left open with no answer.


      **Lawyer reframe.** Dana''s framing is "it''s really just a data migration."
      The reframe is that the migration *is* the regulated event: on day 1 Mosaic
      Relay onboards 252,000 accounts into its own licensed product set with no re-verification,
      repoints monitoring, and launches a cash offer — under an asset-purchase structure
      in which nothing about Harbor''s licenses or compliance record transfers by
      default. The operative question is therefore not "can we inherit Harbor''s status,"
      but **"what must Mosaic obtain, file, decide or preserve in its own name before
      Nov 15, and which parts of the stated deal upside are not actually available
      at close."**


      **Three premises the record lets us test**


      1. *"Just a data migration."* Fails. The day-1 cutover is the moment CIP, licensing,
      monitoring and disclosure obligations attach to 252k accounts.

      2. *"44 states is a nice win — opens four new markets."* Fails on the arithmetic
      and on the law. Harbor 38 + Mosaic 41 with a 44-state union yields **three**
      new states, not four, and the states are never named; and the plan to "use/assume"
      Harbor''s licenses rests on an assumption the record still marks open ([source:ASM-20260909-29b823]),
      against the saved position that transferability should not be relied on without
      a state rule, approval or written regulator position.

      3. *"No re-verification — they were already KYC''d."* Unresolved. Whether Mosaic''s
      own AML/CIP program permits reliance is unknown, and the pre-2023 records cannot
      be recovered (vendor shut down in 2024; only pass/fail survives).


      **Different route the evidence supports.** Run the remaining ~9 weeks as a *gated
      launch*, not a documentation exercise: read and preserve the alert/SAR backlog;
      decide KYC reliance per cohort and schedule remediation; prove or drop the Harbor-only
      states; validate the monitoring cutover with a parallel run; paper notice/consent,
      new customer terms and closing conditions. If a gate fails, migrate only in
      the overlapping states on day 1 and onboard KYC-deficient accounts with limits
      — a scoped migration rather than the full one.


      **Material issues.** Five registered: money transmission licensing (44-state
      footprint); BSA/AML and KYC reliance for pre-2023 users; SAR and alert handling
      (~40 open alerts, unreviewed); monitoring vendor transition at close; $50 welcome
      bonus. Three that are missing and material: **migration data handling and customer
      notice** (the piece the request actually calls "just a data migration," never
      analyzed); **pre-close papering** (closing conditions, interim operation, allocation
      of the alert/SAR and KYC-record risk — no draft or terms appear anywhere); and
      **post-close access to Harbor''s alert/case history** (the records live in the
      SaaS system whose contract ends at close).


      **Three business priorities** — ranked by effect on the business question, time-fixedness
      and irreversibility, not by difficulty:


      1. **Read and preserve the alert/SAR backlog before anything else is scheduled.**
      It is the only item that can change the deal itself; it is entirely unread,
      so no one can yet say whether a filing is late or an account must be excluded;
      and the records needed to answer it may become inaccessible at close.

      2. **Decide KYC reliance for the pre-2023 cohort — rely, re-verify, or restrict
      access.** It determines whether "no re-verification" is available at all for
      the largest population; the underlying documents cannot be recreated; and re-verifying
      or limiting a cohort is a multi-week program that has to be decided before close,
      not after.

      3. **Prove the Harbor-only states can be served at close, or pull them from
      day-1 scope.** It tests the premise the deal is being sold on, state timelines
      are the longest external dependency and cannot be compressed, and serving a
      state without authority is a violation later paperwork cannot undo.


      **Research these first:** the SAR/alert backlog ([source:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38]),
      KYC reliance ([source:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045]), and the licensing position
      for the Harbor-only states ([source:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045]) — in that
      order. If the team needs the earliest single go/no-go decision, licensing converts
      fastest — but it should still follow the backlog read, because a live SAR problem
      can outrank market access.


      **Watch-outs.** The bank-held-funds structure is a saved hypothetical and was
      never adopted; later turns ran under that scenario path, and some prior dossier
      drafts carry scenario scope, so their conclusions are not findings about this
      acquisition. The licensing research has **no citable support** (4 sources retrieved,
      0 passages read; one output headed "No external authority retrieved"), and repeated
      "research queued/running" messages are status, not results. Assumption [source:ASM-20260909-57e86b]
      still calls the structure unconfirmed although the asset purchase is recorded
      and was reconfirmed twice by the user. The matter''s `target_date` field (2026-09-11)
      sits oddly against activity through 2026-09-12 — treat it as unverified. Urgent
      below marks the five items where the close date itself fixes the deadline and
      a mistake cannot be cured afterwards; it is not the same as the top-three ranking.


      *Not performed: no web research. Full-text reads covered the request, facts
      register, intake answers and early analysis; the licensing packet was reviewed
      at excerpt level and prior dossiers treated as fallible synthesis.*


      Dossier research is ready for your choices. No research has started.'

    available_excerpt: '## Preparation note


      **Answer:** Yes. Legal and compliance review is required before the November
      15, 2026 close.


      **Lawyer reframe:** The main question is which findings must become conditions
      to close, migrate customers, or launch in a state.


      The planned 44-state launch is not yet supported. Mosaic should prepare a phased
      launch that excludes the four Harbor-only states unless authority is confirmed.
      The bank-held funds option remains hypothetical. The record does not show that
      it will be ready sooner or solve the other compliance gaps.


      ### Material issues


      - Authority to operate in the four Harbor-only states after an asset purchase.

      - Use of Harbor’s prior identity checks when source documents are missing.

      - Review and ownership of about 40 open alerts and prior suspicious activity
      reports.

      - Continuous transaction monitoring when Harbor’s vendor contract ends.

      - Rights to transfer customer contracts, accounts, balances, and personal data.

      - Legal terms and disclosures for the $50 welcome offer.


      ### Three suggested business priorities


      1. **Confirm the lawful launch area.** Licensing results may require a smaller
      launch or regulator action.

      2. **Make financial-crime controls a migration gate.** Open alerts, missing
      identity records, and monitoring continuity affect the full customer population.

      3. **Protect the customer transfer.** Confirm transfer rights before migration.
      Hold the bonus campaign until the launch area and customer terms are final.


      ### First three issues to research


      1. **Money transmission licensing.** This controls whether Mosaic can launch
      in the four additional states.

      2. **Open alerts and suspicious activity reports.** Existing cases can involve
      time-sensitive duties and irreversible filing or account decisions.

      3. **Monitoring continuity.** Harbor’s current contract ends at close, so a
      control gap could start immediately.


      > A requested saved-record read was unavailable. The writer used the material
      available.


      Dossier research is ready for your choices. No research has started.'

      content: '## Preparation note


        **Answer:** Yes. Legal and compliance review is required before the November
        15, 2026 close.


        **Lawyer reframe:** The main question is which findings must become conditions
        to close, migrate customers, or launch in a state.


        The planned 44-state launch is not yet supported. Mosaic should prepare a
        phased launch that excludes the four Harbor-only states unless authority is
        confirmed. The bank-held funds option remains hypothetical. The record does
        not show that it will be ready sooner or solve the other compliance gaps.


        ### Material issues


        - Authority to operate in the four Harbor-only states after an asset purchase.

        - Use of Harbor’s prior identity checks when source documents are missing.

        - Review and ownership of about 40 open alerts and prior suspicious activity
        reports.

        - Continuous transaction monitoring when Harbor’s vendor contract ends.

        - Rights to transfer customer contracts, accounts, balances, and personal
        data.

        - Legal terms and disclosures for the $50 welcome offer.


        ### Three suggested business priorities


        1. **Confirm the lawful launch area.** Licensing results may require a smaller
        launch or regulator action.

        2. **Make financial-crime controls a migration gate.** Open alerts, missing
        identity records, and monitoring continuity affect the full customer population.

        3. **Protect the customer transfer.** Confirm transfer rights before migration.
        Hold the bonus campaign until the launch area and customer terms are final.


        ### First three issues to research


        1. **Money transmission licensing.** This controls whether Mosaic can launch
        in the four additional states.

        2. **Open alerts and suspicious activity reports.** Existing cases can involve
        time-sensitive duties and irreversible filing or account decisions.

        3. **Monitoring continuity.** Harbor’s current contract ends at close, so
        a control gap could start immediately.


        > A requested saved-record read was unavailable. The writer used the material
        available.


        Dossier research is ready for your choices. No research has started.'

    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md
    available_excerpt: '# Original Request


      From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


      We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
      plan:


      240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
      One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

      No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
      opens four new markets.

      Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
      results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
      Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

      Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
      close+1.

      Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs from
      the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


      Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.'

              text: For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay's own BSA/AML customer identification
                and recordkeeping obligations?

                gap depends on how Mosaic plans to satisfy its own CIP/recordkeeping
                obligations for these users.

              path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-27b344a827f0cf86ced5.md
